This research introduces a comprehensive Java library, LibOPT, that supports optimization tasks through the integration of 59 benchmarking functions, 7 differential evolution (DE) algorithms, and two memetic algorithms (MAs). The process of addressing benchmarking functions within LibOPT is described, and it is made available on GitHub for public scrutiny and utilization.

We have calculated the transitivity degree for complete linearizations of Fano weighted projective spaces with weight triads, as well as other algebraic varieties with a high level of symmetry. Our research builds upon the existing method for computing transitivity degrees in toric varieties and extends it to cover new types of algebraic structures. Furthermore, we investigated the concept of maximal orbit in toric bundles, identifying its key properties and formulating a method to calculate the transitivity degree in these structures. Our findings enable the determination of the transitivity degree in toric Gromoll-Lewy spaces with the largest possible metric dimension.

The paper investigates the behavior of the total momentum operator when applied to multi-particle states in non-abelian setups. The study is built upon a model in which each particle's configuration space is an n-dimensional, compact manifold. The results extend to scenarios with identical interactions across the permutation of any two particles' coordinates. The analysis also examines whether the total momentum operator is well-defined or needs to be substituted with a different operator to describe the system's total momentum. Notably, in cases with identical interactions, a specific approximation emerges in the limit of a large number of particles. The form of this emergent operator is a function of individual particle momenta.

This study investigates the two-photon absorption process within a one-dimensional semiconductor by employing a quantum mechanical model that accounts for the finite width of energy levels and generalised off-resonant conditions. A one-dimensional model is built to describe the transition of an electron within a quantum well and includes the broadening of energy levels in the well, at the band edge, and in the conduction band. By applying the time-dependent perturbation theory, the two-photon transition matrix element is calculated, and the results are presented in the form of an analytical expression for the two-photon absorption coefficient. Additionally, the findings are discussed from a physical perspective and compared with existing models.

We present a study in which we integrate the MARBERT model, which focuses on
modeling social interactions between individuals of different genders, to identify
misogynistic content. Our approach targets three types of misandristic/misogynistic
memes, articles written by trolls, and text containing hate speech. Our findings
demonstrate that MARBERT significantly outperforms other NLP-based detection methods
in its ability to accurately detect misogynistic memes and text containing hate speech.
Additionally, our research reveals that models trained to detect memes perform better
than those trained to process general text.

This research focuses on the solution of a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) whose generator incorporates past values, under specific lip-shaped and growth constraints. Furthermore, a pertinent comparison theorem is established.

Reinforcement learning enables the development of robotic controllers that can operate in uncertain and dynamic settings. Nonetheless, slight variations in the starting conditions or parametric settings can result in unstable performance. Enhancing the robustness of the proposed dynamics model by introducing a minimum threshold for noise levels in the predictive model is explored in this research. Utilizing the random matrix theory's concept of spectral edge, a theoretically grounded approach is applied to accurately estimate upper and lower bounds for noise. By refining the policy through exposure to uncertain data, the suggested strategy effectively reduces misclassification errors. Simulation outcomes for the robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate improved robustness of the policy when applied to the predicted environment.

A recent approach to solving the Kuser N file L demand problem has gained traction for its connection between caching and combinatorial designs, leading to promising developments in the field. We expand upon this research by (i) defining a new set of principles for generalizable coding schemes and (i) exploring connections between these principles and existing coded caching approaches. Our proposed framework offers two key contributions: (i) a methodical way to design general coded caching schemes using a wide array of combinatorial designs, and (ii) an illustration of the link between these principles and existing schemes, including a proof that reveals existing schemes as specific instances of the principles. Furthermore, applying this framework, we introduce the first known general scheme based on non-bipartite combinatorial designs.

This study proposes a Scott model for interpreting predicative languages with multiple levels of universes, aligning with frameworks such as Heyting–Godel and Cumulative Type Universes. We demonstrate the model's suitability for interpreting predicative constructs by formalising it within NatTec and deriving a model of predicative dependent types with large types and small types. Furthermore, this model serves as a foundation for interpreting predicative languages featuring multiple universes, including the development of a core language called Scott Core and its extension with an higher-order dependent language, Scott DSL.

A specific class of degenerate Eisenstein series of weight zero for arithmetic groups acting on the upper half-line is examined, with contributions from Weyl group cosets analogous to those in the adelic framework as described by Brueckner and Yamauchi. It is shown that within this series, only a finite number of non-trivial contributions arise from the affine Weyl group cosets, yielding a distinct expression. This formula serves as a foundational step in deriving the one-dimensional contribution of Eisenstein series towards rankin-siegel relations, specifically in cases of complementary parameters.

This research introduces an innovative method to evade collisions for a type of advanced mobile robotic arm. Building on previous work using spatial information to prevent obstructions, our extension introduces a machine learning approach, specifically a neural network, to optimize collision avoidance. The proposed system leverages the arm's spatial structure and utilizes a dataset of simulated encounters with barriers to create a model capable of predicting paths that bypass obstacles. The results indicate that this method results in smoother motion trajectories with fewer abrupt movements and demonstrates greater effectiveness in more challenging, cramped environments.

To some extent, NLP can be seen as a response to the inherent ambiguity in language, which arises from the diversity of written and spoken forms expressing the same ideas.  This goal, however, is complicated by the additional challenge of understanding language in various contexts, particularly since different forms of expression are often used to convey identical meanings.  This paper explores the feasibility of utilizing a model of dialogue development to facilitate the comprehension of diverse language forms and to facilitate NLP applications, including the generation of a suitable dialogue in light of a particular context.

A key role in quantum metrology is played by the Ramsey interferometry technique. By employing a two-stage quantum gate process, we can create nonlinear interferometers. Introducing a novel class of nonlinear detectors known as nonlinear Hadamard gates, we propose an innovative Ramsey interferometry approach employing nonlinear beam splitters. These specialized nonlinear gates can faithfully reproduce the behavior of conventional linear two-stage linear interferometers but offer superior performance characteristics. As a result, they can outperform the standard Ramsey interferometry using Bose-Einstein condensates. Our research indicates that the novel nonlinear gates are highly practical in real-world applications by accurately mimicking the complexity of linear two-stage linear interferometers while offering improved performance capabilities.

This paper deals with several new value-distribution problems concerning the intersections formed by the images of certain mappings of complex nature with hyperplanes within complex projective spaces. To achieve this, we have developed a combination of a c-infinitesimal approach, a novel infinitesimal result we have discovered, and a generalization of the First Main Theorem from Nevanlinna's theory, which allows us to address these problems. As a consequence, we have derived several significant results.

This work builds upon previous research involving signature-based Gröbner basis algorithms, specifically those for computing a Gröbner basis of a multivariate polynomial system. By exploiting the properties of such a basis, we enable the effective computation of all solution points of a polynomial system with exponential complexity in the number of equations. To achieve this, we integrate all relevant criteria into the basis, thus reducing computational efforts and efficiently determine all solution points.

The PHENIX collaboration's RAPID detector at the BRL measured the rapidity distribution of photons produced in Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=200$ GeV. Findings indicate that the number of rapidity bins with a significant photon yield in Cu+Cu collisions is roughly 1.5 times greater than the number of such bins with a high photon yield in Au+Au collisions at the same energy. This finding implies that the yield of photons per unit of rapidity is greater in Cu+Cu collisions than in Au+Au collisions.

Two functions, exco_2(n,H) and exco_2(sat)(n,H), represent the maximum edges and saturated edges (subhypergraphs satisfying certain properties) in a 4-vertex, 6-edge hypergraph without or with a specific 4-vertex subhypergraph, respectively. Functions are denoted as exco_2(n,H) = exco_2(n, K_4^2 - H) and K_4^2 as the complete 4-vertex hypergraph. Research into these functions has led to findings such as upper bounds on exco_2(n, H) with specific subhypergraphs removed, a lower bound with a polynomial growth, and an initial exploration of the saturated function. Additionally, analogous results were found in the context of list-colorability for uniform hypergraphs.

Rendering complex geometric shapes such as curved lines and symbols poses significant challenges to line drawing algorithms, particularly in terms of accuracy and visual appeal. A traditional approach to rendering these shapes often results in unsatisfactory output due to the inability to preserve roundness and aesthetics. In contrast, a novel method has been devised to effectively render fan-shaped line joins, surpassing the capabilities of existing algorithms in terms of visual appeal and technical feasibility. This method boasts several key advantages, including enhanced rendering efficiency, straightforward roundness control, and an uncomplicated technology implementation. Its validity has been substantiated by the results of unit testing and practical applications.

This study develops a quasi-interpolation formula based on the novel radius-based kernel, a type of radial basis function that remains finite at zero. To achieve this, we first introduce and evaluate the properties of the new kernel. Next, we design an individual function value estimation formula that can maintain convexity, monotonicity, and accuracy for both decreasing and increasing data sequences. Because the RBF has zero non-differentiability points, we also propose an approach to determine the minimum derivative value and show that the derivative formula also maintains monotonicity in certain circumstances. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed formula, we conduct numerical experiments.

The TeV gamma-ray and cosmic ray populations continue to remain unresolved in the central regions of the Milky Way. One possible explanation for this is the presence of pulsar populations contributing to these readouts. In this study, we investigate pulsar halos - extended TeV gamma-ray emission produced by pulsar wind nebulae and the surrounding indistinguishable population of nebulae. By analyzing the Fermi-LAT and HESS data for the central regions of the Milky Way, we place a theoretical upper limit on the contribution of pulsar halos to the TeV gamma-ray and cosmic ray readouts. This data is then compared to the predicted gamma-ray and cosmic ray populations from the surrounding pulsar population. Our findings indicate that the gamma-ray population produced by pulsar halos does not exceed current theoretical models, whereas the corresponding contribution to the TeV cosmic ray population significantly exceeds the range required to account for the cosmic ray population in the central regions of the Milky Way.

This research paper investigates methods to enhance Application Programming Interfaces for Neural Network training, specifically focusing on increasing the efficiency of Data Augmentation techniques. A novel data augmentation technique, Super Pixel Delimiting Masks, is proposed, which utilizes a single image multiple times with different pixel masks to increase the diversity of training data. Another method, Super Pixel Rotation, enables multiple augmented views of each image to be trained. These techniques were evaluated through experiments on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Our findings demonstrate that combining Super Pixel Delimiting Masks with Super Pixel Rotation significantly enhances model performance, outperforming the traditional concatenation of multiple image transformations. Additionally, using our data augmentation techniques allows for the reduction of training time, making it feasible to achieve state-of-the-art results on ImageNet within a shorter training period.

Researchers analyzed climate change as a reference science to examine how different groups perceive and use information from individual to field-level perspectives. They discovered that although climate change information is widely distributed, its overall impact on policymakers is relatively low compared to other groups. Specifically, policymakers display less interest in climate change than general interest science journals or economists. Furthermore, increased attention to climate change within one group does not necessarily translate to other groups, indicating a limited overflow effect. However, climate change as a topic correlates with other prominent groups and topics. These findings highlight the importance of using large-scale data sets to comprehend and address knowledge silos surrounding this critical issue.

Soft robotic systems are increasingly being explored, but their modeling and optimal control remain significant challenges. Utilizing the Koopman operator theory, this research transforms and linearizes a nonlinear multi-agent soft robot system's state, enabling efficient calculation of open-loop and feedback control laws. A case study involving a soft robot actuated by a diode laser and guided through the maze of a maze is examined. The study compares the proposed method with a model-predictive control approach, revealing that feedback law implementation enhances navigation through complex mazes, while open-loop control is only effective for simpler or partially completed mazes.

We present a novel application of the Natural Gradient Descent method to optimize probabilistic neural models, offering an efficient alternative to conventional methods by taking into account probabilities. This reformulation enables the natural gradient to be applied to scenarios not previously addressed in literature, such as Bayesian A/B testing. Our approach significantly accelerates the optimization process, as evidenced by up to 200% faster results in various use-case studies, including Bayesian A/B testing and other high-dimensional parameter optimizations. The proposed method is characterized by its simplicity and generality, allowing for the effective optimization of any probabilistic model without altering its specifications.

At a spectral redshift of 4.5, we've identified two distinct features in the near-infrared spectra of distant active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Although often interpreted as the standard silicon and 2175 Angstrom absorption features, an alternative explanation suggests these are actually Si II at a redshift of 4.5 and Si XIV at a redshift of 5.5. We found the sources of these features to be highly variable, with changes occurring over a period of around 30 days. Additionally, Si XIV features strongly correlate with the blue end of the spectrum, with features observed only when the spectrum is shifted towards the blue by more than 0.15. We also discovered that Si XIV features strongly correlate with the blue end of the spectrum, with features only present when the spectrum is shifted more than 0.15 towards the blue. We also discovered a higher presence of the features in harder-spectrum AGNs. We found X-ray features strongly correlated with the presence of the features, with features only present in harder-spectrum AGNs. We found that the highest X-ray to optical flux ratio is associated with the highest probabilities. Si XIV features strongly correlated with the presence of the features, with features only present in harder-spectrum AGNs.

The time of progression or death of a patient is of significant concern in clinical settings. With the development of deep learning in the field of medical image analysis, researchers have made substantial advancements in the area of radiomics. However, most of the current methods rely on radiological features and clinical data, such as patient's age and tumor size. This is in contrast to CT features, such as airway and nodule characteristics. In order to develop a more effective and lightweight prediction model for the time of progression or death, Lite-ProSENet was created. This model used CT features, such as airway and nodule characteristics, in addition to radiological features and clinical data. Lite-ProSENet achieved an AUC of 0.742, surpassing the existing method with an AUC of 0.694 on the Lung Image Marked Consensus Project (LIDC-IDRI) dataset. This new model can contribute to the development of a efficient and effective tool to help medical professionals in making timely decisions.

Increasingly, researchers are exploring deep learning's potential to decode the brain's language processing areas. However, a key issue with current neural models, particularly those based on a transformer-like architecture, is their lack of clarity when it comes to linguistic interpretation. Although these models excels at tasks like translation and reading comprehension, their inner workings are often obscured by a "black box" effect, making them difficult to understand. To address this limitation, this study investigates whether alternative, more interpretable state representations exist that don't hinder performance in challenging language processing tasks.

Cosmological parameters are inferred from the power spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS). To explore systematics and understand the impact of evolution on the power spectrum, we developed a method to simulate modified realities by manipulating the LSS within full-sky, four-dimensional NBIA (N-body) simulations. LSS four-divergence was altered using a random approach, preserving the primordial gravitational potential fluctuations. This study tested our technique using EBOBB, a sample from the Bolometer Telescope collaboration's simulated data. We applied machine learning models to predict modified four-divergence scenarios, then used them to assess the power spectrum's accuracy and the subsequent bias in cosmological parameter estimation. Our results reveal that at shorter wavelengths, our approach yields systematics in the power spectrum estimate, whereas at longer wavelengths, random model variations result in noisy power spectrum estimates. We also found that, depending on the wavelength, different components of the power spectrum are affected by the algorithm, leading to variations in the estimated cosmological parameters. We also examined the systematics' impact on the inferred parameters, discovering that, depending on the wavelength, various systematics scenarios can either inflate or deflate the total LSS contribution to the power spectrum, thereby modifying the best-fit cosmological parameters.

This brief note aims to establish certain outcomes from the authors' earlier work, 
arXiv:2009.03344, for the sake of determining certain inflection points in tensor 
product formulas. Our current results address the following key questions:

1. In what terms of highest weights can the irreducibility of tensor products 
involving highest weight modules and U(h)-free modules be characterized?

2. How can we identify non-isomorphisms of certain tensor products involving 
highest weight modules and U(h)-free modules under specific conditions?

The effectiveness of long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks is being examined in the context of classifying sentiment expressed in tweets. To address this, a novel approach combining LSTM with a range of word representation techniques has been developed, allowing for the use of existing tweets without the need to alter their content. This strategy involves using words within the context of entire tweets to determine sentiment. The proposed method was tested on three datasets: two that contain emoticons and one that does not. While prior studies often rely on classifying individual words within a tweet, this research demonstrates that an LSTM-based model can successfully identify sentiment without requiring pre-classified words. The technique's effectiveness is further demonstrated by a system design that uses an LSTM-based classifier to automatically detect real-time sentiment in tweets.

In this study, we examine the concept of role specification in conversation systems, exploring its impact on user interaction and overall dialogue quality. Role specification refers to providing operational and stylistic guidelines that a conversation agent should adhere to during interactions. Currently, most studies on role specification in existing conversation systems employ supervised learning methods using annotated datasets. However, these approaches often require significant manual effort to create detailed specifications, which can be limiting.

Inspired by research on style transfer, we investigate whether fine-tuning a pre-trained dialogue model using human annotations can effectively incorporate role specifications and improve performance. Our research primarily focuses on the multi-turn MC scripts dialogue dataset to assess our method's efficacy. Initial findings suggest that utilizing human annotations can positively affect users' perceptions of the conversation agent and elevate dialogue quality, thereby demonstrating the potential to convey nuanced role specifications through supervised learning techniques and possibly enhance existing conversation systems.

Current research on the background of gravitational waves focuses heavily on high-frequency waves, but a significant background of lower-frequency waves, known as the "memory background," has been overlooked. This memory background varies differently with frequency compared to the non-memory wave background. We present two potential sources for the memory background: the memory waves produced by binary mergers and the memory waves resulting from the turbulence in the interstellar medium. Notably, the memory background from turbulent the interstellar medium may dominate over other sources and existing signals. The memory background can significantly change the expected survey results for future detectors like the Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope, which could be detected using a Ainstein Telescope, and the Einstein Telescope, making it possible to confirm its existence and accurately estimate the properties of the interstellar medium and the cosmic evolution.

We show that in models where supersymmetry breaking is driven by a single gauge interaction, there is an intermediate energy scale around a PeV at which supersymmetry is broken, resulting in the origin of matter and neutrino mass. This PeV scale supersymmetry breaking leads to nonthermal right-handed neutrinos being produced through the decays of scalar partners of smuons. As a consequence, we find that the standard model of particle interactions, including the observed properties of neutrinos, is initiated at the same PeV energy range. In our model, the heavy right-handed neutrinos responsible for generating neutrino mass via the seesaw mechanism do not reach their thermal equilibrium, thus avoiding the overproduction of entropy. Nevertheless, we discover a distinct lepton asymmetry is generated by the decays of these neutrinos, a process facilitated by scalar interactions between neutrinos and the scalar partners of up-type quarks. Ultimately, we relate neutrino mass to SUSY breaking, which occurs within the 10^5 to 10^7 GeV range, a range that is testable by supersymmetric particle decays and the property of the lightest supersymmetric particle.

A proposed energy signal processing system utilizes physical layer variables to convey data in the form of energy signal characteristics. We explore how this approach affects wireless communication performance from a semantic perspective. Our findings indicate that the proposed ESL system enhances communication reliability by aligning transmission semantics with channel conditions. Furthermore, we develop an efficient training protocol for channel-aware semantic weighting, which enhances ESL training efficiency. We also propose a semantic communication framework based on deep learning that achieves a significant reduction in computational complexity while maintaining performance close to the original system. Notably, the ESL system demonstrates substantial efficiency improvements over traditional wireless communication systems, achieving this with minimal training data and time.

In this research, our focus is on the analysis of word recommendations made by various models as users type, with a specific aim to investigate the influence of different approaches on this process. By creating a novel dataset that includes hybrid models with the ability to interpret context through syntactic, semantic, and semantic methods, we show that these combined models generally outperform individual ones relying on just one of these aspects. Furthermore, we develop and employ a set of evaluation metrics, including latency, accuracy, and relevance, with the latter assessed through a novel approach that evaluates different types of semantic connections between word pairs, in addition to latency. Through our experiments, we identify areas where various models excel and encounter challenges, offering insights into potential areas for improvement.

In a collaborative filtering framework, attention networks have emerged as a key method for enhancing user model and item encoding, thereby boosting various recommendation tasks. Recent studies have shown that attention networks have numerous variations, and their core concept is to prioritize items relevant to a user's past interactions. However, the specific definition of relevance and a user's past interactions are often unclear. To address this, an innovative, interpretability-enhanced attention network is proposed that integrates rule-based techniques. By forming interpretable rules to define user-item relevance, this attention network network can weigh items based on those rules, effectively enhancing user model and interpretability. Through interpretability, the user model can be refined and invalid rules or unexpected patterns can be identified, ultimately improving both interpretability and the accuracy of the model.

We present analysis of the behavior of flexible-chain dimers and rotors that move through a fluid with a constant energy input, similar to the "effectactive" or "forced" motion, as opposed to "thermal" motion. When a macromolecule behaves like a wheel, the direction it points often influences its movement forward. Similar patterns can be observed in the motion of certain active dimers, which also seem to follow a constant directional direction. However, these biological structures differ from man-made devices, which often move through fluids more efficiently. A common feature among these structures and devices is that their forward progress can be maximized when the "wheels" or the "directional direction" are optimized for their environment. Models that incorporate a constant directional force or torque have been developed to study the motion of such structures. However, these models may not be necessary to explain the motion of active dimers. A common feature among these models is that their motion often seems to be driven by random fluctuations, rather than a constant directional force.

This research presents a novel approach to modeling fractured porous media that incorporates a mixed finite element method for Darcy flow. By ensuring conformity in the mesh's Delaunay tetrahedralization through non-conforming edge extensions, the quality of the mesh is enhanced, thereby improving the accuracy of simulations. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical examples, including the injection and propagation of a viscous front in a fractured media.

This research focuses on achieving stability for a group of drones by using the K-Centroid centering concept. By having a central control system, each drone's target is set to remain at a fixed distance from the central point. This approach leverages the central point's knowledge across the drone network. Ultimately, the goal is to optimize drone group stability and efficiency, enabling applications such as coordinated drone formations and efficient resource distribution. Our findings provide a framework for maintaining stable drone operations, and we have the proof that the central point will converge to minimal movement over time, ensuring steady operations as the drone group grows. This research has implications for various fields using drone groups, such as agriculture, forestry, and air traffic management, offering solutions for efficient agriculture, safe cargo transport, and effective air traffic flow.

The characteristic polynomial of the Seidel matrix of a connected chain graph is determined, and it is found that -1 is always an eigenvalue. A formula for the eigenvalues of this matrix is established, and the polynomial is expressed as a sum of n components. Furthermore, the structure of the eigenvector associated with -1 is identified, and a method for calculating the entries of this eigenvector is provided.

This investigation explores the impact of delays in both state and control variables on a stochastic control problem involving utility optimization for an investor. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, time delays can actually improve optimal investment and consumption rates. To tackle the difficult free cash flow problem resulting from these delays, we develop a solution by utilizing a weak dynamic programming approach that leads to a variational free boundary problem. This problem can be characterized by the differential triple.

Recent research has demonstrated that the eigenvalue problems of the Dirac operator in specific geometries can be linked to well-known mathematical equations, such as Heun's equation or a class of linear difference equations. These difference equations are generated by a diagonalizable, lower (or upper) triangular matrix structure known as a tridiagonal operator. In these cases, the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator correspond to the shift operator and the original tridiagonal operator, respectively. Furthermore, when the eigenvalue problems involve Heun's equation, the tridiagonal operator can be decomposed into two parts: one representing the principal behavior and another associated with a specific, particular solution that impacts the eigenvalues but isn't a solution to the Dirac equation itself. Building upon this research framework, this paper aims to establish a comprehensive set of tridiagonal operators to fully characterize the Dirac spectrum in the scenario of a flat 3D space with a point charge.

In this study, we compare the deployment of base stations and relays in complex vehicle networks to optimize communication performance. We consider a complex network with base stations, relays, and vehicle users, where the base stations and relays are distributed randomly, but the vehicle users follow a pattern known as Poisson-Cluster Process. We focus on two key performance measures: average data transmission rates for vehicles and network coverage. We analyze how these metrics are affected by changes in radio signal strength, base station density, and relay count, by varying them over a wide range. Our analysis shows that using relays can significantly improve network performance, especially in areas with weak base station signals, which is a common issue in these networks.

Our main goal is to develop a high-quality, flexible dataset that can be utilized for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs) in the area of natural language processing (NLP). To achieve this, we collaborated with over 400 volunteers, specifically the editors of Wikipedia in various languages. These editors have the capacity to modify and enhance the quality of thousands of articles, spanning diverse fields and genres. Through their interactions during the editing process, specific sentences are added, removed, or altered. These changes can serve as indicators of the quality of the affected sentences, thus enabling us to create and update a complex dataset comprising various high and low-quality language samples. This collaboration-based approach offers several benefits, including the ability to process a extensive corpus of articles, 100% semantic preservation of the content, and the capacity to process and evaluate the effect of numerous, diverse language models. To facilitate the creation of a dataset, we implemented an approach that utilizes a graph structure to organize and prioritize the additions and deletions of sentences based on the existing and modified article structure. As a result, we were able to involve over half of the Wikipedia editors in the labeling process, resulting in the labeling of approximately thirty thousand articles across twelve different language editions. Specifically, we focused on ten language editions to establish a comprehensive corpus, while specifically involving the Latvian and Lithuanian communities due to the scarcity of available training data in these languages. Each sentence was labeled according to the editing activities performed by

To black-box attack deep learning models using machine, even without access to their training data or source code. A current research approach, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3), creates a virtual model through a simulation that captures aspects of a real model's behavior. Traditional research uses action-based knowledge distillation to teach a smaller model how a larger model behaves, using special techniques like entropy and pairwise distillation. DB3 has numerous challenges due to differences between simulated and actual models. Current approaches that use action-based DB3 suffer from the problems of inaccurate simulations and misleading information. As a result, the trained models are often not capable of reaching their full potential. As an alternative, this paper introduces a novel paradigm called Value-based DB3, which relies on a model's value function to teach smaller models how a larger model behaves. A key component of Value-based DB3 is a special loss function that takes into account both the target class and various classes to reduce the difference between them. Experimental results on public datasets confirm the superior performance of Value-based DB3 on multiple models.

String theory's T-duality exhibits a novel aspect in its application to curved backgrounds, specifically involving line bundles. This relationship is characterized through the lens of twisted K-theory. We demonstrate that continuous-trace algebras serve as an essential framework for representing non-geometric elements of T-duality that arise from gauge fields. Furthermore, the commutative nature of these algebras indicates a one-to-one correspondence between distinct continuous-trace algebras that satisfy T-duality's requirements, implying that duality relates equivalent theories. We derive functional equations for the associated density functions, with the functions on a torus resulting in previously proposed duals. Ultimately, we identify the inherent phase ambiguity within the continuous-trace formulation and propose T-duality as a general transformation applicable to a broad spectrum of string theory backgrounds.

Current reinforcement learning approaches focus on matching expert actions in tasks where multiple examples are available.  However, a few research efforts have proposed training agents with just one demonstration by having them copy the expert's behavior.  Co-imitation learning integrates the advantages of both techniques by enabling agents to learn from a single expert demonstration alongside multiple other agents.  Through our model, we show that information from other agents can be utilized to supplement the expert's demonstration, leading to a substantial improvement in performance compared to existing methods using just a single expert demonstration.  In particular, our approach achieves a 25% improvement over the best single-agent demonstration method in the Clutrr environment.  We also reveal that existing methods that utilize other agents' actions tend to introduce noise, but our co-imitation learning method is capable of filtering out this noise.

We derive an asymptotic expression for the probability of error for a sequential decoder using Polar codes, under the assumption of typical channel inputs, by taking into account the bias parameter and decoder cutoff rate. As a result, we determine the optimal bias value that allows the error probability to decrease exponentially with block length, taking into account the decoder cutoff rate. For lists of polar codes, under the assumption of typical channel inputs, we also derive an asymptotic expression for the error probability of a list sequential decoder, by considering the list length and the decoder cutoff rate. We confirm through simulation that our derived expressions accurately represent the error probability for a broad range of scenarios, including channels where the asymptotic expression is applicable and channels with outliers.

This research introduces a computer vision approach to follow hands as they connect with objects or releases them in a scene. By integrating hands and objects into a unified model, the method allows the network to learn shared features, which in turn leads to more effective tracking during interactions such as when an hand or object is partially hidden from view. It also includes a module to distinguish between hands and objects, and demonstrates through experiments that the proposed method tracks hands and objects individually with greater accuracy compared to existing techniques on standard datasets. Additionally, the proposed approach is shown to have potential in real-world applications, and a video is available at the provided link to showcase its performance.

In 1974, R. building on previous work by D. Gorenstein, completely classified certain groups with specific properties in a finite group context. This presented a comprehensive summary of the existing knowledge. Subsequently, Gorenstein, G. on his own, extended and generalized the results from the original classification, obtaining the forms of reduced groups. This reduced form facilitates easier analysis and understanding of the group's cosets, particularly in the context of its p-subsidiary groups. This current study continues the investigation into the reduced groups of a finite field, successfully classifying a specific type and demonstrating the necessity of the reduced group structure.

A conventional method for calibration typically relies on a single depth sensor to establish relationships between coordinate systems, but its effectiveness can be severely diminished by measurement errors from the individual link sensors. In an effort to make the process more resilient, this research introduces a camera network-based method that utilizes three aligned depth sensors to simultaneously measure a checkerboard target. By leveraging relative measurements between the sensors, the overall calibration process can be significantly improved. Additionally, the use of a depth sensor with superior optical quality to one link further enhances robustness. Notably, this approach brings about a two orders of magnitude reduction in measurement errors when compared to traditional single sensor-based methods.

I investigate how research on the impact of future interventions on existing ones can be extended to multiple scenarios. First, I develop and test a method to identify network interference in eight datasets. This approach selects a key unit of analysis, or 'focal', based on where treatments converge. By doing so, I can detect whether neighboring units are influenced by the treatment. The results reveal that network interference is present in some datasets, but not others. This highlights the importance of choosing the correct focal unit to accurately represent affected units. The method supports both continuous and binary outcomes, and can even identify interference when affected units differ from treated units.

The formation and thermal development of neutron star cores, which occur when dark matter self-annihilates, cause the cooling process to accelerate. This core transformation and the resulting neutron star star formation are investigated, which can occur within a galaxy with or without typical dark matter density. Contrary to expectation, core conversion and neutron star creation can take place in regions with low dark matter density. Core collapse results in a phase transition and produces a substantial amount of thermal energy that's released as a thermal bump during the neutron star's early life. Furthermore, the new cooling mechanism alters and regularizes previously observed irregularities and changes in a neutron star's cooling curve.

The Shapepipe is a C++/Python pipeline that calculates precise and reliable galaxy shapes and magnifications for weak-lensing studies using the Multi-Massification technique. This project is led and customized by N. Battye's group at the University of Cambridge in collaboration with other group members. As an extension of the camera algebra algorithm developed in the LensPipe, the Shapepipe integrates galaxy shape and magnification measurements through a sophisticated algorithm. This code base has evolved from previous work in MGLS and the MGLS2 pipeline.

We address Veech's discrete $2$-circle problem in the hyperbolic plane. Given two geodesic circles with distinct lengths on a modified surface of genus one, we modify the surface by performing a Dehn twist and examine the resulting modified surface. This modification leads to a modified length function for the geodesic flow, and we study its properties, finding that it has only one discrete value, and we construct a flow box that demonstrates this result.

We establish a new method for determining k-rationality in hypersurfaces, improving upon previous work by Voja. Our finding reveals that k-rationality is equivalent to the existence of a particular minimal exponent, which can be expressed as the maximum of minimal exponents arising from key pairs of exponents. This result leads to an effective algorithm for computing the k-Irregularity of k-rational varieties.

We investigate spin-only systems that exhibit square lattice geometry with bond dimers at each vertex, utilizing two recently discovered materials, [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$)$_2$ and Cu$_2$(OH)(pyO)(H$_2$O), both of which exhibit ferromagnetic square lattice dimers. By applying magnetic fields, we observe the suppression of antiferromagnetic spin correlations within the square lattice dimers, leading to a significant shift towards ferromagnetic spin state dimers, particularly in the copper pyrazine material. Furthermore, we analyze various spin state dimers arising from the application of magnetic fields and propose that these findings can be extended to other material systems, including those featuring spin liquid potential and heavy fermion compounds, to oxicuprates under an applied magnetic field.

A comprehensive framework, known as the $\alpha$-Model Standard Model (AUMSM), extends the model by incorporating time-like negative bulk scalars, as proposed in the Randall-Sundrum model with curved backgrounds. In this model, the strong CP problem is addressed, the electroweak vacuum is stabilized with an appropriate cutoff scale, and the Hierarchy problem is resolved while adhering to experimental constraints on extra dimensions.

Quantic provides an online cloud-based quantum computer with access to 64-qubit devices featuring various types of gates, including Clifford, non-Clifford (T), and measurement functionalities. By combining these elements, quantum circuits can be built to replicate the outputs of complex algorithms like Shor's, achieving an $O(\log N)$ scaling of probability approximations with $O(\log N)$ qumes. Our device-level classical simulation achieves high accuracy, achieving a total variation distance of around $10^{-3}$ at 45-depths on circuits consisting of random single-qubit rotations, followed by a depth of T gates. This places our simulation tool on par with the most advanced simulation software in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Our simulation outperforms existing methods in handling a greater variety of quantum circuit components.

This study focuses on the holographic dark energy model derived from Tsallis statistics.  Based on the non-extensive statistical mechanics, a generalization of the UV cutoff scale has been proposed, and its effect on the cosmological scale has been given, and finally, a scale of dark energy has been obtained. We have also examined the cosmological phase diagram, and have found a transition from one phase to another, and have found it to be dependent on the model's parameters, and finally, it has been found that the parameters are related to each other, and this relationship has been found to be $y \approx 1.34x$, and this relationship has been found to $S-1 \approx 0.34(\gamma-1)$, and this has been confirmed.

The Chinese Distant Sky Survey's Local Area Meteorological Optical Sky Telescope (LAMOST-TDS) commenced operations in 2018. A comprehensive dataset was gathered over a 4-year span, covering 4666996 time-exposures and 5369896 spectral readings. To facilitate the study of binary systems across 36699996 binary fields, we designed and executed the LAMOST-TDS program. The data reduction process yielded 36699996 binary entries, of which 36699996 showed binary characteristics. Out of these, 36699996 included an active component and 36699996 an inactive component. The data analysis revealed 36699996 binary systems with a total mass ratio. Consequently, the LAMOST-TDS program has successfully cataloged 36699996 binary systems. Furthermore, the data have enabled the detection of 36699996 long-period binary entries, of which 36699996 have a period exceeding 1000 days. Notably, our findings have identified and cataloged various binary system types such as symbiotic systems, contact systems, and other unique binary configurations.

The role of a True Random Number Generator (TRNG) is crucial in various applications, requiring numerous random numbers. Existing TRNG solutions fall short in processing high-volume random numbers simultaneously due to their sequential operation. The TuRaN (Tunable random number generator) is a novel, on-chip TRNG that utilizes a single, highly capacity-rich ring laser oscillator, whose frequency is converted using a digital circuit. The use of a single optical source and conversion circuit results in the TRNG's high throughput and low energy consumption. With an impressive data rate of 3.5 Gbps, the 700-um ring laser TRNG consuming 12 mW has demonstrated superior randomness and passed a comprehensive battery of industry standard and research tests. When generating a batch of random numbers, the TuRaN's per-bit energy is 1746 times lower than that of an electronic quantum TRNG.

We have developed a novel resistive switch based on the ON/OFF current properties of a single-electron tunneling device. Developed using a simplified fabrication process, it was used in a simple oscillator circuit to study its zero-temperature frequency behavior. Additionally, a simulation model was created to investigate frequency dependencies and estimate a single-electron tunneling timer's maximum achievable frequency. Utilizing electron-pumping methods, we were able to power the oscillator with an external voltage, as well as control its frequency through an electric field, independent of circuit capacitance. When the switch operated near a resonance condition, an anomalous increase in frequency was observed, with values one order of magnitude higher than previously reported single-electron tunneling timers. Moreover, this resistive switch exhibited current characteristics suitable for integration into more complex circuits, such as single-electron memory systems.

The application of Feynman integrand causal representations has proven valuable in massless one-loop and massless and massive two-loop calculations due to its capacity to capture loop topological structures through factorization properties. In this context, we extend this concept to the analysis of two-loop scalar Feynman integrands with a general topology, and explore its implications for the interpretation of loop topological diagrams. Furthermore, we examine the causal representation's capacity to represent massive effects.

This study examines the connection between the $U$-UW spectral measure and the Green functions of the discrete Laplacian on various subsets of the/described by $\mathbb{N}^d$, such as finite intervals, trees, and more. Green functions and their derivatives for these subsets are found to be expressible in closed forms. These structural characteristics are crucial in establishing that the /U-UW spectral measure in dimensions $d \geq 3$ is discrete, with the aim of presenting a simpler proof in comparison to an existing one [arXiv:1509.01604]. Additionally, a simpler derivation of a result from [U. UVW] is also presented.

Researchers have used star mass and radius data to investigate how two distinct physical descriptions, the quark mixed chiral bag model and the color superconducturing 2-flavor color superconductur model, interact within the stars. By creating 126 possible star compositions with varying internal structures, they analyzed data from three stars to find the most likely parameters. Two, four, and five of these models best fit the data, leading to new insights into star densities. These findings highlight the importance of considering multiple physical descriptions to understand the inner workings of these stars.

We are investigating an optomechanical system that integrates a q-deformed beam splitter with an optomechanical amplifier. The system's dynamics are influenced by tunneling, which is modified due to q-deformation. Our analysis reveals that tuning tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling allows for control over tunneling direction and is essential for achieving steady states. Additionally, we observe that the system can produce non-Gordon-Watson (GGSW) behavior under specific conditions related to q-deformation. Furthermore, we examine the quantum state of the mechanical oscillator and find that the system's steady state exhibits steady quantum state cooling under certain parameters.

This study focuses on a specific type of collective state known as scissors modes, comparing both standard (R-positive) and unusual (R-negative) varieties within the experimental dataset from isomeric beam experiments on Xenon-108. A theoretical investigation, involving large-scale calculations based on the projected projected valued interaction, has yielded distinct characteristics for R-negative states. Specifically, these unusual modes exhibit notably lower electromagnetic transition strengths compared to their R-positive counterparts, but are associated with significantly larger mechanical transition parameters.

This investigation examines the phenomenon of thickness-induced metal-insulator transitions through electronic and percolation models, using a single-layer hexagonal boron nitride as a case in point. A comprehensive analysis incorporating electrostatic interactions and band structure effects is carried out to explore the intrinsic properties of this material. Additionally, percolation theory and its modifications to account for the specific case of hexagonal boron nitride are explored to calculate the resulting insulator metal transition. A thorough study of the band structure reveals a natural thickness metal-insulator transition occurring at natural thickness and above, with space charge-induced phenomena resulting in further transitions at sub-natural thickness levels. A comparative study through ab-initio calculations validates the predicted transitions. Based on the model, a practical guide is developed for achieving the metal-insulator transitions in hexagonal boron nitride via chemical vapor deposition growth.

Recently, researchers have observed significant deviations from standard statistical patterns in large groups of laser-cooled and trapped atoms. These deviations exhibit the characteristic "low count, high probability" and "high count, low probability" tails seen in a class of heavy, fractal distributions known as discrete scale-invariant (DSI) or power-law.

A theoretical framework is presented that explains the occurrence of these power-law patterns in systems governed by linear dynamics. This DSI distribution arises when there's a random variation in the timing of these linear responses, and is shown to be similar to the Pareto distribution.

Applying this understanding to atomic ensembles, it is demonstrated that the power-law effect can occur due to the inherent time-dependent interactions within the ensemble, as measured by the system's energy levels and size.

Following the global pandemic-driven decline, the cryptocurrency market experienced significant growth in the first half of 2021, driven by surging prices and increased trading volumes. This resurgence led to a heightened interest in digital assets, particularly among retail investors. To investigate these phenomena, researchers analyzed data from leading crypto platforms and trading instruments. By constructing a trading network, they were able to map the relationships and interactions among cryptocurrency traders during this period. Their findings revealed a complex network with distinct clusters corresponding to distinct trading submarkets. As prices and trading volumes increased, the traders' connectivity decreased, resulting in fragmented trading groups with reduced interactions. This study underscores the importance of trading network analysis in understanding market dynamics and monitoring trading behavior, thereby contributing to a deeper comprehension of market mechanisms.

A combined approach of ab-initio and path-integral simulations is applied to examine the reaction of a proton transferring from H2SO4 to a combination of one to three water molecules. Within the data set, the motion of protons in a quantum state at rest is considered and compared to its classical counterpart.  The results show that the motion in a quantum state of rest significantly impacts class-III water molecules but has minimal impact on protons transferred to one to two class-I/II water molecules.  However, this motion plays a more significant role when protons transfer to two class-I/II water molecules simultaneously.

Consider operators that preserve distance and remain unchanged under the action of a group on a complete metric space. Our research focuses on situations where the space of possible changes is both uniform across the space and unchanged under the group's action, and we prove that it can be represented as a part of a certain compact space with specific properties. If the space has specific characteristics, such as being simply connected and having a connected collection of local features, then the operator representation includes all possible changes within the space. This result has found an application in the study of invariant neural networks that maintain distance, which can be embedded in a part of a compact neural network with specific properties.

A comprehensive molecular dynamics study, spanning hundreds of nanoseconds, delves into molecular transport within a confined microchannel with a spatially varying temperature profile to test the applicability of the Einstein relation. A thorough analysis of the hydrodynamic region reveals temperature-dependent diffusion coefficients that significantly deviate from the predictions of the Einstein relation, a widely accepted viewpoint in molecular transport with limited investigation in low-dimensional systems. A novel, simulation-based approach to treating finite-temperature diffusion, rooted in statistical mechanics, is then proposed to correctly interpret these results, and it is found to accurately describe the diffusion coefficient at various temperature gradients. Furthermore, a direct comparison between the simulated diffusion and the heat flow via molecular thermal conductivity confirms the validity of the generalized Einstein relation, a key component of the Green-Kirkwood-Boussinesq theory, and an important basis for modeling molecular transport in nanostructured heat-tuned devices.

Recent studies have uncovered a critical relationship between deep learning training and generalization, emphasizing the role of various training techniques in reducing model complexity and improving performance. It has been observed that different optimization methods can lead to models with distinct structures, such as localized dependencies between parameters. This paper investigates how specific training heuristics like parameter norm regularization or decoupled optimization affect model complexity in deep neural networks, such as convolutional neural networks and VGG16. The analysis focuses on the impact of these training techniques on the complexity of the localized graph representation of the model. The study also explores the effects of training on convolutional kernels, weight sharing, and the reproducibility of results through controlled numerical experiments.

This study presents a cross-section measurement for the rare decay $\bar{D}^0$ $\to$ $e^+$ $\nu_e$ using data collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to 1.75 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. An unbinned maximum likelihood fit was applied to enhance accuracy in extracting physical parameters, resulting in the decay's branching fraction being determined with statistical significance and yielding a result of (1.34 $\pm$ 0.61 $\pm$ 0.54) $\times$ 10$^{-1}$ in agreement with the standard model prediction.

The availability of quality training data is crucial for developing accurate and efficient models, including those for automated essay grading. Access to domain-specific training data can be challenging, thus data augmentation techniques that enhance data quantity and diversity are of significant value. In this research, we investigate data augmentation techniques, including those based on text summarization, to improve automated essay grading. We developed a novel method that combines text summarization with the expansion of essays to create modified versions, which are then used to train a grading model. This strategy demonstrates improved performance compared to existing grading models, particularly in cases where training data is limited. Additionally, our data augmentation technique exhibits minimal negative effects on the accuracy of a grading model when applied to a dataset with ample data.

We investigate methods for assessing two classes of models based on marginal independence estimates, focusing on Gaussian copula models and general copula models. For the first class, we investigate exponential weighting estimators that can be used to test Gaussian copula models and estimate their parameters, and for the second class, we develop an entropy approach for testing copula models with various constraints, such as those based on Markov structures, and prove consistency and rate of convergence for both methods. Our results are supported by numerical simulations, which also demonstrate the potential use of our methods in a high-dimensional setting.

The distribution of societal opportunities significantly influences long-term social structure, yet existing models fail to account for this impact on future generations. We present a model where multiple generations, each consisting of diverse individuals, interact over time, with some making decisions and others enjoying opportunities within the system. These models identify conditions for the persistence of opportunities and demonstrate that, in the absence of such persistence, systems converge towards equilibrium. Moreover, it is shown that opportunities' cessation within the model leads to a particular type of inequality pattern. We examine various scenarios, including the allocation of opportunities to the poor, the middle class, or the wealthy, and analyze the intergeneration consequences of each case. Our analysis indicates that allocating opportunities to the poor or the middle class leads to the convergence of systems towards a balanced state, with equilibrium systems exhibiting a moderate level of inequality. Conversely, allocating opportunities to the wealthy results in systems converging towards a system without such allocations.

According to the spin-statistics theorem, wave functions representing multiple identical particles with a given total non-negative integer spin S must acquire a specific sign factor, (-1)^S, when the coordinates of any two particles are swapped. In this study, a mathematical proof for this theorem is provided for systems of n identical particles in a d-dimensional space (where d >= 1) with a potential that depends on the relative distances between particles. The proof involves a continuity argument and the solution's extension to a cover of the permutation group.

The rise of cryptocurrency necessitates peer-to-peer transactions on a network, but as more users and transactions grow, achieving scalability, anonymity, and trustlessness becomes increasingly difficult. To tackle this challenge, our project introduces an innovation called Delegated RingCT, which allows for faster transactions, lower fees, and quicker block validation times of under 100 milliseconds. Delegation involves a trusted entity, known as the delegator, that assists in validating transactions and blocks, with fees going directly to this delegator. Our approach combines advanced cryptography, specifically Grothendieck-Riemann-Silhold theorem and isogeny-based signatures, from side channels, preventing side-channel attacks, from the delegator.

For any constant $\epsilon > 0, $ we analyze the complexity class $\text{AA}^{(s)}_\epsilon$ which encompasses problems that can be solved using circuits with polynomial size, non-uniform depth $s$, and approximate solution generators for linear systems that have an error margin of at most $\epsilon$.
For the case of uniform circuits, our findings show that each approximate solver in polynomial-time can be transformed into a reduction that involves decreasing either the error rate or the circuit depth, much like previously observed reductions for exact solvers in terms of circuit size and depth.
Furthermore, non-uniform circuit reductions between approximate solvers can be expressed through a comparison of circuit sizes and depths.
These circuit-based insights yield new insights into the relative power of approximate linear system solutions at different circuit depths.
Specifically, for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $0 < \delta < 1 - \epsilon$, there exists a constant-depth circuit family $\mathcal{C}^{(s)}_\delta$ that can solve any linear system of size $\tilde{O}(n)$ in time $\epsilon + \delta$, which indicates an efficient circuit approach to solving large linear systems with a small error margin.
This construction involves a combination of reductions between approximate linear system solutions at circuit depths $s$ and $s+1$ and a simple modification to the resulting circuit.
