Our analysis covers the individual and combined measurements of the gauge bosons WWW and WWZ in the energy range up to 1.2 TeV, utilizing the data gathered from the 2011 and 2012 running periods with the ATLAS detector at the LHC, based on an 8 TeV proton-proton collision and a total integrated luminosity of 25.0 fb^-1. The observation of these boson events is based the identification and reconstruction of specific final states, including combinations of three or four leptons and highly energetic momentum carried away by jets or the absence of such momentum. After analyzing the data, we find the production rates of WWW and WWZ to be 16.1% and 13.1% higher than the predictions made by the standard model, respectively. The corresponding discrepancies between the measured and predicted cross-sections are 5 and 3 standard deviations.

The last two decades have seen significant growth in Natural Language Processing for Hebrew. This growth is documented in a comprehensive report that analyzes advancements in NLP for Hebrew and related languages over time. Notable improvements are observed in the field's state-of-the-art results and the resources available for NLP in Hebrew. A new UD treebank (UDHE) has significantly boosted the state-of-the-art performance on NLP tasks in Hebrew. NLP models that leverage transfer learning and pre-trained word embeddings have achieved impressive outcomes, particularly in text classification challenges. Despite these advancements, specific areas like question answering, narrative understanding, and anaphora resolution still require further development. Although several pre-trained models and frameworks have been released, there is a need for more support for domain-specific applications and multilingual resources. NLP for Hebrew continues to make valuable contributions to the broader field of NLP, highlighting the potential of less-resourced languages.

J. Bourgain demonstrated in 1989 that Epsilon-isometric dimension reduction by linear operators is feasible for Banach space unit balls that have Epsilon-isometric dimension reduction by affine Epsilon-isometric embeddings but not for Convex sets in general. This restriction was further refined to Polytopes. Our research extends this discovery to other types of sets, including those that are both Star-shaped and Epsilon-asymmetric. Furthermore, our findings show that even sets exhibiting a minimal degree of asymmetry cannot undergo linear dimension reduction in the same manner, despite allowing affine dimension reduction. Notably, all these results rely on the property of asymmetry, whereas previous results for Convex sets depend on a combination of convexity and asymmetry. Consequently, our findings address the individual impact of convexity and asymmetry in dimension reduction, following the example set by B. Lindenstrauss, who showed that properties 1) and 2) cannot always be interchanged by considering appropriate examples.

Convolutional neural networks are highly effective in solving problems involving elasto-plasticity, but they are not well-suited for problems involving plasticity, elasto-plasticity, and problems with evolving plastic behavior, as these require a form of memory that CNNs do not inherently provide. To address this limitation, we develop a continual learning approach that enables the use of convolutional layers in problems with evolving plasticity, including all types of history-dependent plasticity models, without requiring an excessive amount of data. By incorporating this method into the solution of elasto-plastic problems, we allow for the addition of evolving plastic variables as continuation variables and for problems to be solved using the alternating direction method of multipliers in an operator learning framework. As a result, this approach benefits problems that can be solved with constant convolutional layers, such as those involving monotone history-dependent plasticity with evolving hardening, but also those with more complex models like kinematic, mixed isotropic/kinematic hardening, and Bilinear Kinematic Isotropic Hardening (B31) models.

Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, particularly when their parity-check matrices exhibit a property known as negative degree-degree correlation, are known to be more resilient to channel noise.  It has been discovered that modules from the graph representing these codes can be exploited to determine their maximum tolerance to erasures.  Preserving the property of negative degree-degree correlation through module splicing results in an LDPC code with equivalent error-resilience.  Furthermore, it has been established that sparse graph representations, consisting of interconnected subgraphs, of certain terminated check-node graphs, are also characterized by negative degree-degree correlation.

This note introduces the Optimal Musiako-MPC scheme, a method for controlling linear systems with constraints and unpredictable limitations. Our approach, denoted as SL-MPSF, efficiently handles this scheme by leveraging a pre-computed quadratic value function and a quickly calculational feedback control. The use of SL-MPSF ensures system safety by maintaining compliance with all constraints, while also optimizing problem parameters outside of the real-time control loop. The stability of SL-MPSF is rigorously proven under conditions of bounded disturbances.

We propose a newly discovered attack on quantum key distribution using both vacuum and weak decoy states, employing only extremely low power from the eavesdropper, which cannot be detected. This "very weak attack," based on a specific configuration of signal states, exploits a vulnerability in the mean value calculation used during the protocol. We demonstrate that the very weak attack can outperform other methods, even with advanced techniques for detecting anomalies, and discuss its implications on the security analysis of QKD using this technique. Additionally, we outline modifications to the security analysis that may mitigate this type of attack.

There has been significant interest in few-shot in-context learning for NLP, with research focusing on improving the performance of pre-trained models in this area. Despite a lack of models that consistently excel in this field, the issue of which natural language models are best suited for few-shot in-context learning remains underexplored. We investigate whether the common practice of selecting models based on their performance on a single task can be justified. Our study comprises two parts. Firstly, we create a new, comprehensive dataset with a wide range of few-shot in-context learning tasks. Secondly, with this dataset, we conduct the most extensive study to our knowledge on the link between the performance of pre-trained models on task-specific training and their low perplexity. We find that there is no definitive correlation between the models' perplexity and their performance in few-shot in-context learning, which suggests that the choice of a pre-trained model for this purpose should not be solely based on its performance on a single task.

We've studied the impact of anisotropic thermal conductivity on the inversion instability in galaxy clusters using numerical simulations. These simulations involve continuous inflow of cold, gas-rich infall from surrounding regions. Our findings show that continuous inflow leads to significantly enhanced instability growth, with a much higher amplitude compared to its discontinuous counterpart, a phenomenon previously observed in these systems. Notably, our results reveal that the growth and amplitude of the instability are notably increased when employing anisotropic thermal conductivity. These findings have significant implications for the inflation of radio halos and the evolution of large-scale structures within galaxy clusters.

Recent experiments have provided valuable data on beauty baryons and rare meson decays, as well as novel insights into charge parity violation within these systems and charm mesons. This report summarizes the current status of these developments, with a focus on theoretical advancements related to the observed anomalies.

We have developed fresh formulae for the scattering of four string bits in the high-energy regime, confirming and strengthening prior conjectures. Our findings indicate that these new amplitudes obey all string theory symmetries, specifically those involving the exchange of external states and the interchange of internal bit states. Furthermore, the derived formulae pass rigorous tests for unitarity, a key principle in quantum field theory, by explicitly highlighting the high-energy resonance patterns that ensure the validity of the amplitude. Notably, the new results reveal a distinct pattern of resonances that was absent in the earlier conjecture. Interestingly, as the number of bits increases, the high-energy four-point amplitudes seem to converge towards the Virasoro-Shapiro amplitude, the standard scattering amplitude for a string.

This work addresses the task of optimizing edge computing facilities by developing a machine learning-based approach that takes into account dynamic user access patterns. A dataset is presented, formed from a combination of synthetic and real traffic information, to enable the study of this problem. Our proposed optimization framework, rooted in queueing theory, balances user satisfaction and energy efficiency. Furthermore, two deep learning models are proposed to forecast dynamic traffic patterns. By integrating this forecasting strategy with a day-and-night pattern, two novel machine learning-driven methods for task assignment are presented, demonstrating their potential to enhance ECF performance in terms of energy efficiency, user satisfaction, and nightly rest. Notably, the input data requirements for user requests are minimal. Importantly, the optimized ECF can achieve energy savings of up to 47% and up to 65% reduction in energy during day-time operations, while also significantly reducing workload at night.

Most speech synthesis models focus on choosing an optimal encoder to group speech segments into clusters, allowing for local voice changes. However, it's observed that some parts of the encoder retain too much speech information, making it difficult to transition smoothly between clusters. To address this, a two-part approach is proposed. The first part selects a good encoder using a training objective that emphasizes the importance of energy, spectral, and duration features. The training involves two stages: unsupervised learning of an encoder and voice-specific refinement. The second stage involves decoding an chosen encoded speech into output speech, allowing for steady and transient components. Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate that the proposed encoder outperforms existing approaches in enabling pitch-controlled cross-voice synthesis and produces more controlled speech with chosen-encoded noise.

This work addresses the development of motion planning for robots with multiple limbs. Due to complex dynamics, producing feasible motion plans is extremely challenging. We developed an advanced optimization method that incorporates multiple stages, using simplified, pre-computed paths as a starting point to drive more detailed optimization. This method's performance and computational efficiency were evaluated and shown to be comparable to stage-specific optimization, but significantly faster. Additionally, we modelled any planned motion as a sequence of connected segments, allowing for the exploration of alternative paths through continuous deformation. This approach enables optimization of both individual segments and their overall sequence. Our approach was validated using various robot configurations, including those with three and four limbs.

In various applications, there is a necessity to obtain numerous copies of an ideal quantum state from less-optimal ones, a process known as purification, with its opposite, maximally resourceful state extraction, called distillation. A distilled state's quality and rate are typically defined by its fidelity, with fidelity being the sole focus in previous research, except for specific scenarios. This paper, however, generalizes this idea by presenting a distorted fidelity framework that characterizes the trade-offs between error rates and outcomes in distillation processes. Introducing a concept of $\alpha$-fidelity, we relate it to existing fidelity measures and provide distance measures in the underlying state space. A key technique involves a joint normal form representation, enabling us to address the asymptotic quantum distillation process, determine the distance measure, and solve the single-shot and large-block fidelity scenarios.

This study examines the dynamic movements of a coffee cup when it's subjected to horizontal and vertical forces. By altering the position of the pivot point, various effects emerge. If the pivot is positioned directly beneath the cup, simply oscillating it vertically causes the coffee to settle rapidly within a few seconds. Oscillating the pivot in any other direction causes the coffee's surface to adopt nonlinear characteristics. If the pivot point is positioned a short distance away from the coffee's center, changing the oscillation direction from vertical to horizontal can actually reduce the coffee's nonlinear motion.

We are examining the performance of distributed stochastic gradient descent using bound projection methods. Specifically, we investigate the circularly-constrained optimization problem, where multiple devices with circularly-constrained models attempt to converge on a convex differentiable function. We evaluate two bound projection methods - midpoint gradient descent and a new variant, double descent, for solving this constraint optimization problem. We first analyze these methods in an exact setting, then introduce a inexact version, known as DR-DSGD, by approximating the midpoint gradient in this framework. Analyzing the convergence of DR-DSGD, we find that it can reach an $\epsilon$-precision solution within $O(\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{K}\sqrt{N}\log(1/\epsilon))$ iterations, involving a constraint modulus, condition number, network size and log accuracy. We also examine the efficiency of concurrent updates, by introducing a modulus squared assumption, which yields the first linear convergence rate $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{K}\sqrt{N}\log(1/\epsilon))$ for convex optimization using DR-DSGD. Finally, we verify the feasibility of our novel modulus assumption using an empirical convex optimization test on a large circular constraint.

The rapid rates of nucleus-nucleus collisions in heavy ion experiments result in a highly non-equilibrium state. Our novel, entropy-conserving model simulates the evolution of matter from its initial, pre-equilibrium phase all the way to the final state, encompassing both the non-ideal and ideal phases of fluid dynamics. By conserving entropy across these phases and matching the anisotropic particle momenta, we derive a universal relationship between the pre-equilibrium phase and the resulting charged particle yields in the center-of-momentum frame. This model also accounts for the temperature dependence of the initial state and non-ideal fluid properties on the final state. When applied to the ALICE data on lead-lead collisions, the parameter-free model accurately reproduces the experimental results for minimum bias and high-multiplicity events in the range of 7 TeV to 62.5 GeV.

A theoretical model was used to examine how a one-dimensional envelope's early mass accretion phase proceeds, both with and without magnetic fields present. The model, simplified for computational efficiency, assumes rotational support for the envelope and employs a 3D magnetohydrodynamics code to simulate mass inflow from a fixed inner boundary to an adjustable outer boundary with accompanying mass ejection at both poles. These simulations, which varied alpha-viscosity values and magnetic pressure forces, revealed that a critical point exists where mass ejection ceases at approximately 0.035 times the envelope outer radius in units of the mass ejection timescale. Below this critical point, the mass ejection timescale remains roughly constant at 2000 times the orbital period, and the mass ejection rate is found to significantly exceed the mass accretion rate by a factor of two, suggesting that mass ejection plays a crucial role in the mass loss process during protostar formation.

We suggest a method to counteract the impact of non-stabilizing variables in complex systems, by introducing a feedforward compensation mechanism for variables that accelerate system instability. This is achievable through a controller, which can serve as an "anti-fragile" system, to mitigate the effects of these variables. Our proposed framework can be applied to model a wide range of systems that exhibit both stabilizing and non-stabilizing dynamics. This framework includes both linear and affine systems, as well as higher-order nonlinear systems that can be linearized around an operating point. This method may also have implications for safety engineering concepts such as "Safety in Orange" and systems that are inherently safe by design.

An uncontrolled object may experience significant changes in orientation and tilt due to the interaction between solar pressure and orbital resonances, leading to potential collisions. To predict these changes, researchers created low-thrust, high-eccentricity and high-inclination orbits, which accurately simulate the effect of solar pressure. By using this approach, they found that orbital characteristics can be successfully reproduced with minimal error, even without including higher-order gravitational effects. Additionally, they identified the source of discrepancies, which are primarily attributed to the choice of reference plane. Furthermore, they analyzed the sensitivity of solar pressure models to variations in the object's orientation, which is crucial since this information may be difficult to obtain precisely.

We investigate the performance of the electromagnetic response in tight-binding models, particularly in relation to the electromagnetic vector potential and gauge methods, using a two-dimensional tight-binding model of the Hall cliff effect as an example. It becomes apparent that the gauge is incapable of accurately capturing the spectral electromagnetic response, leading to significant discrepancies in the calculated Hall conductance. To overcome these limitations, we propose two potential approaches: first, using both the velocity and gauge to construct the electromagnetic response, which yields correct results at low energies; second, transforming the gauge into a gauge well-suited for describing the electromagnetic response in a sum-over paths framework. Notably, this novel gauge exhibits singularities at zone boundaries, necessitating modifications to the path integration to account for this. Our analysis also sheds light on the influence of the tight-binding cutoff on the Hall conductance, offering valuable insights into electro-magnetic tight-binding models and their applications.

The research develops a novel statistical model, grounded in graph theory and Bayesian estimation with robust parameters, to simultaneously calculate object pose, form, and cluster data in the presence of significant outliers. Unlike existing robust methods, this approach can handle a large number of outliers without requiring prior knowledge. Graph theory is utilized to partition feature correspondences and determine which features to ignore, while a Bayesian framework determines the optimal number of clusters. Additionally, the study puts forth a theory that outlines the conditions under which the optimization problem has a unique solution, and proposes an algorithm to resolve this problem. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the method on various synthetic and real-world datasets, including estimating the 3D structure of objects, groups, and surfaces.

We consider the multivariate location model in complex space $\mathbb{C}^p$, and develop a confidence region for a $p$-dimensional Cauchy distribution. This region corresponds to a sphere, whose radius and center are determined by the data, and it is important to note that this region may also be represented as a ball in the imaginary component of $\mathbb{R}^{2p}$. This finding has practical implications for image processing and computer vision applications.

Large-scale clinical trials often require substantial funding and a significant regulatory and commercial burden.  A key aspect of a successful trial is the statistical design, which needs to be both adaptable to clinical changes and adhere to regulatory standards.  Within clinal trials, multiple treatments or backgrounds are often compared.  This paper explores how to optimize these comparisons by borrowing information from background treatments that are not directly involved in the main comparison.  By using a multivariate adaptive response design, we can increase the power of our analysis and reduce the required sample size.  Our findings indicate that even borrowing from non-commensurate subgroups can significantly reduce sample size requirements, while multivariate adaptive designs provide up to a 35% reduction in sample size for commensurate subgroups.  The approach is compared to other common designs and found to be at least as effective as the best of them, with notable gains over other adaptive designs.

This study investigates how spatial variations in dynamics affect motion control tracking performance. Most contemporary motion control feedback systems utilize PID algorithms due to their ease of implementation, yet they fall short in capturing the underlying dynamics due to their position-independent nature. To address this limitation, a controller designer must either utilize more intricate models or adopt iterative tuning methods, such as loop-shaping on a linearized model or trial-and-error adjustments, however these methods prove laborious and cumbersome. To simplify this process, this paper introduces a new area rule integration technique that enables the precise calculation of dynamics parameters from measured response data, specifically for systems featuring pairwise balanced dynamics. By transforming these parameters into a form suitable for use in a quadratic cost optimal controller, this study facilitates the design and implementation of an optimal controller that accounts for positional dynamics variations. Furthermore, this study examines and analyzes how closely actual positional tracking will follow the planned trajectory under the influence of external disturbances, sensor inaccuracies, and other unforeseen factors.

We develop a novel approach that leverages the encoded features from a deep learning model for point cloud registration. This feature-based method not only serves as a preliminary step in registering point clouds, but also enables the incorporation of these features for various downstream tasks, including object classification. While the extracted features may be influenced by point sampling, we design the model to be sample-robust. Experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness and sample robustness of the proposed approach.

Let's consider $\mathcal{N} = \mathcal{N}(\mathbb{Q})$ as the collection of all solvable rational matrices of degree $n \ge 1$. The set $\mathcal{N}$ forms a subgroup within $GL_n(\mathbb{Q})$. The centralizer $C_{c}(\mathcal{N})$ in $GL_n(\mathbb{Q})$ relative to $\mathcal{N}$, contains invertible rational matrices that commute with lower triangular matrices with $1$ on the diagonal and arbitrary entries above the diagonal.

In the given article, the centralizer $C_{c}(\mathcal{N})$ in $GL_n(\mathbb{Q})$ relative to $\mathcal{N}$ is identified and the following properties are studied: the centralizer $C(\mathcal{U})$ in $GL_n(\mathbb{Q})$ relative to the subgroup $\mathcal{U}$, consisting of strictly upper triangular matrices with $1$ on the diagonal; the centralizer $C_{c}(\mathcal{S})$ in $GL_n(\mathbb{Q})$ relative to the subgroup $\mathcal{S}$ of permutation matrices; and finally, the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of the group $G = C(\mathcal{U}) \times C(\mathcal{S})$ is studied

A comprehensive and accurate measurement of the top quark mass is crucial for further research on top quark properties, its decay mechanism, and potential new physics. A compact e+e- collider or a muon collider demonstrator can achieve one percent precision in top quark mass measurement through event by event mass reconstruction and sophisticated analysis techniques. Alternatively, an advanced detector at a high-energy collider has considerable potential to achieve the same level of precision in top quark mass measurement, offering an unexpected opportunity for this difficult task. We examine the feasibility of achieving a top quark mass measurement precise to 1% at each of these facilities and compare their relative merits.

One key aspect of studying materials using ultrafast light experiments involves analyzing data from transmission or reflection spectra to trace the progression of excited electronic states over time. We developed a new method to trace these excited states by using data from all wavelengths simultaneously, as opposed to analyzing each wavelength separately. This method is highly efficient and can effectively handle experimental data that contains noise. We tested our method on synthetic data and real experiments, including studies of a material with a simple optical response and another exhibiting complex behavior with multiple absorbing and emitting bands in the visible spectrum.

Utilizing a relativistic quark-gluon model with an effective bifermion mass operator,
we examine the twist-3 quark-globuon distribution amplitudes for the $\rho$, $\rho^*$,
and $D^*_s$ mesons, finding that the transverse polarization components are heavily
suppressed, on the order of $10^{-2}$ for $\rho$ and $10^{-1}$ for $D^*_s$. Moreover,
at large momenta, the longitudinal quarks contribute more to the DA than the small
component quarks, with the small component quarks' contributions being approximately
$0.1$ of the total for $\rho$, $0.2$ for $\rho^*$, and $0.05$ for $D^*_s$. These findings
are in line with perturbative QCD predictions and current Lattice QCD simulations.

We investigate the growth characteristics of functions within Gelfand-Shilov spaces and their Fourier transforms through a stepwise approach, where each step corresponds to a specific class. To establish accurate growth estimates, we consider the best possible norms and rely on the result that these coefficients obey factorial asymptotics. Consequently, we derive estimates of a function based on the behavior of its Fourier coefficients and vice versa, specifically the $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ and $S'_{\alpha,\beta}$ classes, and thus prove analogous estimates for their Fourier transforms.

This paper presents an innovative instance segmentation approach, called Co-creative Segmentations GAN (CoSGAN), that generates multiple, precise instance segmentation masks for an image, adaptively tailored to each image's content. CoSGAN achieves a single shared instance segmentation prediction (SSP) and multiple personalized outputs through a collaborative learning framework. To enable the generation of precise segmentation masks, our model employs a boundary-aware decoder that uses global image features. By sharing high-level instance features, our approach improves the quality of SSP and personalized predictions. CoSGAN demonstrates superior performance on the MS COCO benchmark, setting new state-of-the-art standards in both instance accuracy and novelty detection.

Human action anticipation poses a significant challenge in the field, as many existing methods struggle with spatial translation issues and offer little to no temporal context, resulting in unsatisfactory performance at early time frames. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that integrates movement landmarks, local spatial patterns, and temporal dynamics to enhance early time frame predictions. Specifically, we employ a two-stage process: first, we extract temporal features through an efficient architecture that leverages both 2D and 3W cues from video data; second, we synthesize a global movement signal by interpolating radial basis function kernel values at significant movement landmarks. Finally, we establish meaningful connections between signal components using a motion-sensitive model, which yields enhanced early time frame accuracy. This approach achieved record-breaking 50ms joint action recognition performance on the 50MT-Challenge 2020 dataset.

Recent studies on the rare star AD Leo reveal that it experiences frequent, powerful flares, either in the optical or far-ultraviolet spectrum, often peaking at extremely high levels of intensity, far exceeding those seen in the Sun. High-resolution spectroscopic data taken during two significant flares, however, showed the hydrogen spectral lines didn't broaden as expected, indicating the spectral lines formed in regions unaffected by the intense stellar wind. This study delves into the complexities of studying stellar wind diagnostics using the stellar activity spectrum.

We have discovered new, non-trivial IMA Riemannian and K\"ahlerian examples. Additionally, our analysis shows that all abelian instantons exhibit a specific property of having an extensive kernel. Furthermore, we found a unique method for constructing solitons from IMA Riemannian and K\"ahlerian examples through the use of a simple gauge transformation. It has also been shown that the properties of G2-instantons, solitons, and the self-duality equation are fully characterized by an equivalent system.

To establish the normality of operators, we initially define the concept of a normal operator with respect to a coherent vector. Subsequently, we determine the precise conditions for normality of composition and weighted composition operators acting on the Fock space.

The $s$-core, $t$-core, $s$-ple $p$-core and $t$-ple $p$-core of a partition $\lambda$ are defined as those partitions that share the same number of nodes in the same relative $s$-th, $s$-th, $t$-th and $t$-th positions respectively, where the number of nodes in the same relative $s$-th, $s$-th, $t$-th and $t$-th positions is the same for all nodes in the same relative $s$-th, $s$-th, $t$-th and $t$-th positions is the same for all nodes in the same relative $s$-th, $s$-th, $t$-th and $t$-th positions. In this paper, the authors focus on the study of the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions of a partition $\lambda$ and establish that such a partition is periodic with a fixed period of $p+1$ in the number line. In addition, the authors derive a formula for the number of the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions of a partition $\lambda$ in terms of the number of the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions of a partition $\lambda$ in the number line.

Deep learning models for three-dimensional point clouds are increasingly being used in machine vision applications such as self-driving cars and robotics. As these systems handle sensitive tasks, ensuring the reliability and security of these point cloud models is of utmost importance. The transformation properties in three-dimensional space pose a significant challenge, where small disturbances can lead to significant changes in the data's geometry. In this research, we introduce the Trusted Certified Protection (TPC) framework for three-dimensional point clouds, enhancing and certifying the accuracy of models against potential threats. Our framework consists of three components: Safe Projection for Data (SPD), Moving Hyper-Box (MHB), and Adversarial Region Shrinking (ARS). The Safe Projection Data framework ensures the security of models by projecting perturbed point clouds into a limited safe space. Additionally, the Moving Hyper-Box framework boosts the efficiency of the adversarial training process. Furthermore, the Adversarial Region Shrinking framework aids in creating a more accurate model with reduced training costs. Extensive experiments using multiple datasets demonstrate that the TPC framework costs less computationally and offers higher accuracy compared to existing methods.

This paper presents an assessment of system performance for a network employing Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar, where multiple sensing networks operate in a shared environment, generating interference through splayed chirps. A theoretical framework is developed to calculate the probability of interference caused by splayed chirps, followed by the derivation of a network throughput formula. This analysis enables the evaluation of how key parameters such as chirp density per packet, sweep duration, and network size impact interference probabilities and throughput. A recommended optimization technique is introduced to identify the ideal chirp density that maximizes network efficiency by balancing retransmission costs and interference-induced packet loss. Iridium, an uplink-based FMCW radar network utilizing submillimeter wave communication, serves as the primary case study to illustrate theoretical findings and guide design decisions through simulation.

A Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram's visibility holds vital information about a quantum phenomenon known as entangled two-photon absorption. This phenomenon can be found in certain quantum materials that absorb photons. The visibility can help us learn more about how these materials interact with light on a non-linear level. The volume of research in this area is rapidly growing due to its potential applications in photovoltaics and quantum communication. To accurately measure this visibility, certain trade-offs between signal strength and noise must be managed effectively. We outline a method for estimating this visibility by analyzing third-order correlation functions using a maximum-likelihood approach. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through experimental data from a study on ruby.

Let $T$ be a one-dimensional torus, and let $E$ be a complex elliptic curve that does not have complex multiplication, with complex multiplication by the ring of Hessian integers. We derive a one-dimensional torus $T$-invariant elliptic cohomology theory, denoted as $E\ell l_T(E)$, using the methods of Roberts and Lurie in their elliptic spectra constructions. This theory is based on an elliptic spectrum $E\ell l(E)$, which we also define. Furthermore, we investigate the topos of sheaves for the Galois group of $E$-over$\mathbb{C}$, denoted as $\Gamma_E$, as well as the one belonging to the anisotropic form of $E$ over $\mathbb{R}$, denoted as $\Gamma_{E/\mathbb{R}}$. Finally, we prove that $E\ell l(E)$ splits in both topos settings.

In temporal knowledge graphs, encoding entities and relations with time-sensitive numerical values is crucial. However, the current method of using time intervals to calculate embeddings overlooks an entity's or a relation's state changes between time points. To address this, we've created a novel time-encoding scheme that takes into account an entity's or a relation's state transitions. This is done by visually representing the temporal information as coordinate coordinates and using Bezier curves to fit the data. The time-encoding vector for each point is then calculated based on the curve. To accurately capture local entity or relation state changes, we've introduced the concept of temporal neighborhoods and tested our framework's effectiveness by designing two versions of the temporal neighborhood. The experimental results show that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, with improvements of 5.6% to 12.6% and 2.0% to 7.0% respectively. All relevant code, data, and models have been made publicly available at https://github.com/med-ai-lab/CA-TKGC.

When an object collides with the ground, the resulting sound can sometimes be heard both above and below the ground surface. In this study, a comprehensive mathematical model is presented, explaining under which conditions the sound from the impact is heard below the ground and on other planets. The model takes into account two primary factors: the material's ability to transmit sound and the angle at which the object hits the ground. The object's sound transmission through the ground is explained using both high and low frequency regimes models, especially on other planets. A detailed analysis is conducted on three specific scenarios, including Earth with typical ground materials, Earth with ice and snow, and other planets with diverse materials.

Systems exhibiting flat bands, characterized by high degeneracy and unique properties, often display robustness to deformations when viewed through a geometric or topological lens, but can be susceptible to breaking symmetry in certain cases. Topological protection generally fails when the band structure breaks its underlying spatial inversion symmetry, an effect that also breaks degeneracy in system models. Our initial focus was on understanding how randomness impacts degeneracy in these models, discovering that random bond disorder tends to maintain degeneracy, whereas randomness in on-site potentials causes the gap to remain open near the band edge but results in a fully localized state at the band center. However, broad randomness of chiral potentials preserves degeneracy, consistent with the principle of chiral symmetry. These findings specifically apply to square lattices featuring a su(2) spin degree of freedom, yet raise questions about how these results extend to other lattice systems with multiple degrees of freedom.

Research on two-dimensional (2D) materials has gained momentum due to its potential in developing next-generation devices. The study of electron-phonon interaction in these materials is crucial to understanding their properties. The two-dimensional (2D) hydrogen boride monolayer (BM) exhibits a honeycomb crystal structure, making BM an ideal candidate for investigation. By employing the density functional perturbation theory and ab initio approach, the acoustic and optical phonon bands, electronic band gaps, and electron-phonon coupling constant were calculated. The results indicate that hydrogen plays a significant role in the interactions within BM. Furthermore, BM exhibits a high sensitivity to biaxial strain, with the band gap being modulated through strain. The inclusion of hydrogen within BM results in notable enhancements to the electron-phonon coupling, strain sensitivity, phonon frequencies, and band gap size. BM's exceptional acoustic phonon speed makes it potentially useful in phononic applications. BM's outstanding properties make it an excellent candidate for practical applications, including phonon transport, phononics, and the development of van der Waals heterostructures, as well as ultra-wide bandgap and high-resistivity materials.

We investigate a specific type of flattened partition, focusing on the number of instances where the sum of a set of positive integers equals n, with the largest element being at most k. When excluding the number 1 from these integers, we develop a recursive formula to calculate this count, denoted as $f_{n, k}$. Furthermore, we derive a set of closed-form equations to understand the relationship between these integers, specifically the number of instances where the sum of a set of k integers equals n, excluding the number 1, with a corresponding set of recursive formulas to calculate this count.

We analyze finite type actions of finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups on space of characters of their finite quotients, and find parallels with dynamics on tori. These groups' action behavior can be understood using rational rank, yielding results like equivalence of orbit closures under rational rank invariance and characterizing closed orbit structures. Results rely on properties of Voronoi cells and show distinct differences from finite rank abelian group actions on their space of quotients.

Evaluating the functional safety of automotive driving systems typically involves two steps: functional safety analysis and random testing. However, model checking offers a formal method to assess functional safety with greater reliability. This paper presents a model checking approach that validates the safety standards of controller area network systems, which forms the backbone for distributed automotive electronic control systems. We also explore how the high level of abstraction used in model checking can contribute to safety case documentation, thereby streamlining the safety case preparation process.

The complexity of nonlinear dynamics in numerous applied fields defies comprehensive analytical understanding. In the field of analysis, a prominent approach to modeling dynamical systems is the Koopman operator. This framework linearizes dynamics through an observation-based lens. However, identifying these operators often relies on restrictive assumptions or is limited to specific systems. To address this, we devised an expanded, unified approach to dynamic inference using the finite Koopman operator. By incorporating a neural network into the process, our proposal allows for the efficient approximation of these operators. Consequently, we established the feasibility of approximating nonlinear dynamics within bounded domains. The proposed method was empirically evaluated on both synthetic and real-world systems.

During the 18th century, many scholars, particularly those with anti-Leibnizian views, perceived a stark divide between bounded and unbounded infinities, often attributing this dichotomy to Leibniz. Despite their misinterpretation, our research indicates that Leibniz, in fact, consistently regarded all instances of infinity, whether in quantity or in divisibility, as either unbounded or derivative from it. By clarifying these misunderstandings, we aim to present a comprehensive and modern view of Leibniz's philosophy of divisibility and actual infinity, resolving long-standing philosophical debates within the framework of the Scholastic principles of continuity and greatness.

I investigated how the removal of foreground signals and noise reduction techniques affect the cosmic microwave background (CMB) parameter estimates. Utilizing the Planer tool, which simulates CMB maps by stripping away foreground signals, and modifying it to include signal-to-noise ratio optimization, I analyzed the impact on the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect and CMB lensing power spectra. Followed by an examination of the impact on the cosmic microwave background reionization parameter $\tau_{\rm eff}$ when using Planer or CSBM maps instead of real CSM maps. My results show that foreground removal has a relatively small impact on CMB power spectrum and lensing parameter estimates. However, when estimating the reionization parameter from Planer or CSBM maps, a small bias is observed, but it decreases with an increasing number of maps in a simulated dataset.

Consider an infinite-dimensional vector space V over a field K that has an orthonormal basis (e_n). Let's say we have an operator T from V to V, and for every positive integer k, the vector sequence (T^k(e_n)) consists of linearly independent vectors. Our findings indicate that, for these vectors to be orthonormal as well, they must satisfy a specific mathematical relationship, similar to (T(e_n)) = (e_n).

Over time, there has been a significant increase in the quality and quantity of data available for training recommender systems. Nevertheless, such systems rely heavily on high-quality data and their effectiveness can significantly decline when faced with data shortfalls or inconsistencies. To address this, researchers have concentrated on developing methods that can utilize text-based document information to construct more comprehensive user profiles and improve recommendation quality. These innovations have led to better performance in homophilous and interpersonal settings, and there is now an need to evaluate their efficacy in other crucial aspects of recommender systems, particularly when dealing with data scarcity and the challenge of cold-start. To this end, we present the first benchmark of 10 document modeling-based methods that yield satisfactory results for both collaborative filtering and the integration of content and collaborative signals in a complex setting. Through an in-depth analysis, we have found that, on average, these methods outperform traditional and content-based recommender systems by 6.5% and 3.8% respectively, and we have also identified potential areas for enhancing the robustness of document modeling in diverse scenarios.

This paper investigates the connection between conditional freeness in probability and asymptotic behavior in random matrix theory. We establish a novel method to approximate finite-dimensional matrices using freely and conditionally mixed subalgebras from non-commutative probability theory. This approach leverages conditional freeness to interpret the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues or singular values of large random or deterministic matrices, given certain matrix classes such as diagonal or Toeplitz.

Our study refines and improves existing random matrix models, particularly those involving ratios of Toeplitz matrices, by incorporating a more nuanced approach. By applying asymptotic distribution results to a matrix ensemble derived from freely or conditionally mixed matrix ratios, we are able to reproduce and extend the results of Zhang and Yin for large symmetric Toeplitz matrix ratios and an extended class of Toeplitz matrix inverses.

The general framework of our method also enables the analysis of more intricate matrix constructions, such as sums of inverses of random Toeplitz matrices, which were previously only yield a first-order asymptotic distribution.

Systems requiring timely responses must continuously monitor their environment and adapt accordingly. Given the unpredictability of time in practical applications, it is essential to devise monitoring strategies that can cope with time variations and failures. Moreover, since no single approach to time is universally applicable, it is crucial to develop monitoring frameworks that are- or at least consistent with- consistent with specific time modeling models. This paper explores this issue by defining three monitoring strategies timely, timely+, and timed++- and verifying their correctness with respect to a particular time modeling model. Additionally, the paper provides a practical implementation of these strategies and an empirical assessment showing that, although timely+ and timed++ monitoring offer improved accuracy over timely monitoring, timed++ has the highest level of correctness.

Researchers searched for the exotic tetraquark state $aa\bar{a}$ formed by two up, one down and one strange quarks through the decay of an $A_2$ or $I=0$ $\rho$ meson, accompanied by an $a_0(980)$ resonance. The analysis, based on $36.1$ fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at $13\,$TeV, found no significant evidence to support this search, and the resulting 95\% confidence level upper limit for the related process is $3.4 \times 10^{-4}$ for the branching ratio.

We've detailed the methods for calculating two key levels of stabilization parameters for the GRAVITY interferometer, which significantly enhances its performance in several ways. Firstly, by focusing on specific aspects, these parameters minimize systematic errors and streamline the data analysis process, thereby reducing its computational complexity to a level proportional to $N$ measurements. Secondly, their real-time calculation allows for an effective utilization of the main control system and the availability of $6$ additional stabilization parameters. Our approach has been successfully implemented using $2$ dedicated cameras, which have been crucial in optimizing the instrument's operations and will remain relevant for the instrument's entire lifecycle.

A core objective in cluster analysis is the $k$-center problem which seeks to minimize the maximum distance from any point to its nearest cluster center, given a budget of $k$ centers. In its capacitated variant, the challenge is compounded by the requirement to cover at least $k$ centers in the process. Notably, approximation algorithms with a factor of $(1 + \ln n)$ have been achieved in Euclidean spaces, and further progress was made with a factor of 2 in general metrics by Berman et al. (STOC 2020).

This study delves into the computational complexity of solving the problem within classes defined by their structural properties, characterized by the parameter $k$ representing the number of centers, and dimensionality parameter capturing structures within the input. The main discovery is that, assuming the P != NP condition, achieving optimal polynomial-time approximations for the problem with highway dimension under certain conditions is impossible, and we explore the influence of these parameters on the problem's approximability using advanced tools, including diagonalizers.

We've demonstrated that for entire functions of class $f$, which satisfy the equation $(\Delta^m P(f) + Q(f))\Delta^{n}Q(f) + P(f)^{l} = c$, with $m, n$, and $c$ being positive integers, and $P$ and $Q$ being polynomials of degree one with $P(1) 
eq 0$ and $Q(1) 
eq 0$, and under the condition that $T_ho(Q, r)$ is less than $T_ho(f, r)$ for a sufficiently large $r$, if the composite function $(\Delta^m P(f) + Q(f))\Delta^{n}Q(f) + P(f)^{l}$ shares the value 0 with its shifted version $((\Delta^m P(f) + Q(f))\Delta^{n}Q(f) + P(f)^{l})^\circ z + \eta$ for $0

This research presents an modified version of a well-known algorithm for solving polynomial linear systems, inspired by Kalmar's work. The algorithm recovers polynomial linear systems in a manner similar to Reed-Solomon erasure code decoding by employing an interpolation approach. Like Guruswami and Kumar's method, Kalmar's algorithm utilizes a finite field extension to handle errors and also employs an iterative technique. We have developed a new method that avoids the need for multiple field extensions, instead using an existing field extension and performing it just once. This method can solve a system of equations with n vectors and k entries over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with up to $\lceil q/2 \rceil$ errors, as long as the number of unknowns k exceeds the product of n and the error count. This method represents the most efficient solution currently known for this error limit. The method can be applied to the multivariate polynomial least squares problem, a common issue in cryptography and coding theory, in a list decoding manner. This leads to the development of a new, more efficient multivariate polynomial interpolation approach that is applicable when a finite number of input-output pairs is available, even in the presence of significant errors.

In this work, the controlled emission of entangled correlated photons in the form of photon pairs is investigated within a cavity QED framework consisting of a two-level atom and a quantum dot as the interacting particles. The sequential excitation of the system leads to the controlled production of entangled photons, with its polarization, via the cavity. Even and odd correlated photons are distinguished based on the number of photons in the system, and their joint polarization correlations are examined. Moreover, the temporal evolution of the entangled photons' density matrix reveals the loss of polarization entanglement due to dephasing over time.

By applying advanced density functional theory to four alkali metals under extreme pressure conditions, we have found that the existing equations of state need significant improvement to accurately reflect the behavior of these elements at high pressures. A new theoretical model, supporting the idea that all alkali metals behave similarly under high pressure, has been proposed and validated. However, this model, like the proposed state equation, does not take into account the subtle differences in interatomic forces, resulting in a slight overestimation of the pressure requirements for phase transitions. Accurate predictions of the pressure requirements for a phase transition in potassium, necessitating revised adjustments to the proposed model. Ab initio calculations of interatomic forces indicate the possibility that a zone correction is necessary, especially considering the presence of anisotropy resulting from lattice distortions. Determining the accuracy of DFT in predicting total energies, as opposed to just interatomic forces, remains a crucial area for further research and validation.

The formation of local parity breaking domains within hot and dense nuclear media, such as those resembling a chiral magnetic effect, could significantly impact the mass spectrum of vector mesons. The primary objective of our work lies in the systematic examination of the vector meson mass shift within such a medium, taking into account that it breaks parity locally and thus possesses a distinct vector and tensor vector component. Through a perturbative QCD analysis, we have derived, to the leading order, the mass shift of the vector meson, which, in the presence of parity breaking, separates into distinct electric and magnetic components. This separation, a direct consequence of the Chern-Simons term, results in an anomalous magnetic moment for the vector meson.

This paper addresses size estimation over a undirected distributed network, where each node begins with a random number, with only the leader having access to the total size of the network, no node has a global identifier, and the network is composed of a Turing-incomplete model. A novel, randomized distributed algorithm is proposed that achieves precise size estimation with high probability in networks that contain at least one fully connected component, utilizing an adaptive and controlled data aggregation process that converges in a number of rounds that is logarithmically proportional to the network size, which is also applicable in the worst-case network scenarios. A series of theoretical proofs are developed to validate the correctness of the algorithm. A numerical simulation is conducted with various types of network structures to demonstrate the performance of the algorithm.

A novel approach to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint in variationally incomplete regions is presented, stemming from the conformal transverse regularization scheme. Unlike standard methods, this scheme does not necessitate a lapse, and the Hamiltonian constraint is solved by gradually increasing the conformal factor from a conformal boundary, initially treated as complete. The resulting, incomplete boundary is then smoothed into a complete variationally complete region, and the lapse is solved by addressing the resulting Hamiltonian constraint and momentum constraints. The resultant complete region's boundary is then replaced by a gravitational field, and its completeness is验证ed through the Karch-Radou equation.

The main chamber of the JUNo neutrino research facility will house a massive array of 20,000 optical detectors, each containing a 20-ton water-based scintillator.  For a long time, researchers have been working toward the JUNo detector's ultimate goal of precisely measuring the neutrino oscillation mass order.  A key element of the detector is its Event-Grade Photomultiplier, or EGPM, which must operate reliably for decades.  So far, the SUCCESS experiment, utilizing 30-ton EGPMs, has been successfully running for 20 years without fail.  However, the EGPM technology behind the SUCCESS experiment is out-of-date and doesn't meet the level of performance required for the full-scale JUNo detector.  Therefore, newer and superior photomultiplier technology must be developed and tested to meet the demands of the JUNo detector's final configuration.  A crucial aspect of the newer EGPM design involves its supply chain, which will need to be carefully coordinated and managed for a 30-year project.  To support the eventual JUNo detector's final configuration, over 16,000 optimized EGPMs, incorporating advanced EGPM design parameters, will need to be produced.  A thorough analysis and research into the近30年 photomultiplier supply chain for the JUNo research facility will ensure the successful completion of the project.

In multidimensional time series forecasting tasks, the existing Informer model often underperforms due to its inability to effectively process input sequences, leading to suboptimal inter-series correlations. This challenge becomes particularly pronounced when dealing with complex series that cannot be represented by a single dimension. This paper introduces an enhanced Informer model, I2Informer, to address this limitation. Firstly, the I2Informer I2Informer model leverages a 3D encoder to self-attention relationships between different dimensions within input sequences, thus improving inter-series correlations. Secondly, the model utilizes a linear output layer instead of a fully connected one in the decoder, as this reduces output dimensions and minimizes information loss. Experimental outcomes confirm the I2Informer model's superior performance in forecasting multidimensional time series.

Advanced ADC designs need to precisely convert incoming photons into electronic noise-equivalent electrons. As a result, the choice of atmospheric models is crucial in such ADC designs. Various researchers have proposed different atmospheric models, prompting a necessity to select an optimal model according to the specific ADC parameters. By comparing several established atmospheric models, we found the MODTRAN model does not provide the best results, particularly for blue wavelengths. Consequently, we developed an empirical atmospheric model based on the AM1.5 solar spectrum, resulting in up to 1000 times better agreement for low-impact ADC designs.

Combining multiple models often yields superior performance, but the common application of simple averaging, which ignores model confidence, can be suboptimal. A more effective approach, Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), was developed to address this issue. PILE uses the pairwise differences of labels, which can be computed efficiently, to inform its fusion process. By recursively applying an iterative logistic regression on the model pair differences, PILE identifies and leverages the characteristics of the ensemble more effectively. As a direct consequence of this approach, PILE can be combined with any model that outputs uncalibrated soft probabilities. Furthermore, PILE enables transparent inspection of its ensemble learning process through visualization of the activated features. Our study demonstrates PILE's efficacy on 17 tasks, including 10 pre-training and fine-tuning experiments, by outperforming other ensemble methods and providing insights into its benefits.

We investigate an expanded experiment setup consisting of LIGO's twin detectors to detect ultralight matter made of bosonic particles. Our analysis focuses on the collective benefits offered by a network of sensors in enhancing detection capabilities and sensitivity for particles that interact weakly with ordinary matter, resulting in reduced signal intensity. Additionally, we examine various data analysis techniques, including methods that leverage multiple detectors and account for differing sensitivities, as well as a post-processing method that evaluates the coherence of data from different detectors and combines their data, giving more weight to the more sensitive detectors. We find that the network approach can significantly improve detection sensitivity by up to a factor of two, depending on the detectors' coherence and relative sensitivities. Furthermore, we develop an optimized "inverse-variance weighting" weighting function that provides a more sensitive estimation of intensity, which can be more sensitive by as much as 40% compared to simple averaging, with the level of improvement varying based on the detectors' relative sensitivities.

The complexity of the basis pursuit problem, a method for finding the sparest solution to an underdetermined linear system with noise, is closely tied to the properties of a specific matrix, particularly the relationship between its spectrum and the condition number. A recent study proposed a relationship between this number and the feasibility of efficiently recovering sparse vectors through novel algorithms. Building upon this idea, we establish connections between basis pursuit performance and the distribution of eigenvalues in A, also examining the representability of sparse vectors in certain nonnegative definite matrices. The potential applications of our findings to Riemannian basis pursuit are then explored, offering significant advantages such as robustness to arbitrary linear transformations and reduced computational complexity.

This paper outlines key areas of research and development in programmable switch technology, with a focus on the emerging challenges and opportunities within this field. The rise of programmable switches has enabled innovative applications in areas like network performance monitoring, security, data plane programming, in-band network addressing, and more. However, a significant barrier to progress is the scarcity of open-source compiler backends, which hinders reproducibility and further research within the community. Due to this limitation, existing cases often lack generalizability and the potential for new ideas is restricted. To address these issues, this paper discusses specific areas requiring attention and provides potential research directions, with a particular emphasis on promoting open-source tools, designing performance-monitoring tools, developing efficient networking languages, ensuring network stability, and creating reliable testing methods.

The study compares two methods for solving the vector transport equation in a general grid format, a standard method based on a linear solver and a method using a mixed finite element formulation with an exponential solver. They explore how different finite element formulations and solvers impact the performance of vector transport operations, and test various decoupling strategies for the nonlinear system. Ultimately, a high-performance algorithm is developed by combining these components, and its efficiency is demonstrated through a case study of a large simulation involving unstructured mesh vectorization, to be used in a real application, with details reserved for a subsequent publication.

Machine learning techniques such as fairness metrics, federated learning and differential privacy can effectively address concerns about privacy and ethical considerations. This paper provides an in-depth comparison of these three approaches from a theoretical standpoint.

A LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV, which were recorded with the detector, to investigate the $B_c^+$ particle. By analyzing the production $B_c^+Baryon\,\bar{\textit{b}}\rightarrow X_b+Baryon\,\bar{\textit{b}}$ in an excited state, researchers found two excited $B_c^+$ states, $B_c(2S)$ and $B_c(3S)$, which were both $1^+$ in spin. Their masses were determined to be 6545.8 and 6601.3 MeV, respectively. This analysis, which was based on an analysis of the invariant-mass spectrum of certain particles, led to the observation of these excited $B_c^+$ states, which were both $1^+$ in spin. Their masses were found to be 6545.8 and 6601.3 MeV, respectively.

Stage I-2 Runge-Kutta methods can be applied to solve initial value problems with continuous variables and are analogous to general linear methods for discrete variables, but with additional flexibility due to their continuous nature. When applied to oscilatory Hamiltonian problems, the precision of such methods can be enhanced by choosing withdrawal points that correspond to the integration quadrature points, thus optimizing the number of withdrawal points to be more than one. This choice can lead to symplectic and oscillatory-stable solutions, which are crucial for accurately integrating Hamiltonian systems over long time periods. The precision of the Hamiltonian total energy evaluation is also increased with this choice, possibly leading to more precise energy values than those obtained with other methods.

This research introduces a novel approach to critic training, where the critic is trained in a localized manner by utilizing gradient information that bypasses the convolutional and recurrent layers of the policy network, thus significantly reducing computational costs. Experiments demonstrate that the local critic method yields policy improvements on par with full-trained critics, while accelerating training process for deep convolutional and recurrent neural networks by 2.4 to 3.7 times, without incurring a loss in performance.

We investigate the impact of non-conservative flow on three distinct types of chaotic scattering and compute measures of their sensitivity to initial conditions. The study focuses on a map derived from the Hopf bifurcation and and utilizes metrics such as the Lypovexit exponent and fractal dimension to analyze the boundaries of basins of attraction. It is observed that weak dissipation renders all Wada basins in the dynamic system stable, yet remains undetectable through the calculated metrics. Conversely, dissipation significantly alters the boundaries of three basins in another dynamic system, rendering them invariant under its variations. The minimal chaos identified through these experiments corresponds to a scenario where three regions interact in a specific sequence and is characterized by a fractal structure with a fixed exponent and index, respectively.

The muon g-2 collaboration recently reported significant evidence for new physics, suggesting a hidden scalar particle, potentially linked to its own decay. To further explore potential connections with the muon g-2 anomaly, an experimental collaboration has proposed producing this hypothetical scalar at the muon proton collider (MuPC) through the reaction $\mu^+ p\to \mu^- X$. Estimations indicate the MoMuCosmo, a future muon beam test facility at the CERN ISOLDE, has the capability to investigate parameter ranges that could explain the muon g-2 results and the mass of the scalar, with its muon beam characteristics closely resembling those planned for the full-scale MuPC.
