The detection of large numbers of exoplanets in the K band by a specialized telescope has expanded our knowledge of planetary systems around Sun-like stars. This research examines the mineralogy and internal composition of planets similar to Earth that orbit within the habitable zones of M-dwarfs and Sun-like stars using a specialized model. The model is validated against existing data and then applied to analyze exoplanets discovered by the Euclid space mission and a future mission led by a 6-meter telescope. The internal structure of these small planets is found to be complicated, with multiple boundaries and a core composed primarily of metallic rock. However, the addition of water significantly alters this structure. Stars like our Sun have a thicker crust and a mantle rich in silicon, whereas smaller, cooler m-dwarfs produce Earth-like planets with significant water content. As a result, their interiors have a core-mantle structure with little water in the mantle. Ultimately, this core composition has a substantial impact on the mineralogy and internal structure of their mantles. Ultimately, the type of star influencing a planet's internal composition has significant implications for its seismic activity, magnetic field, and biological potential.

This work explores attention mechanisms for channel feature learning in wireless communications, starting with analyzing how attention mechanisms process channel information in massive MIMO systems in a deep learning framework. An attention-based CSI learning method is developed to enhance performance in massive MIMO systems, and an innovative metric is designed to measure the contribution of each attention mechanism. This metric guides a model reordering mechanism to accelerate training without sacrificing accuracy. Additionally, we investigate how reducing CSI precision via quantization impacts the attention mechanism's performance. An efficient mechanism for real-world systems is proposed to let a trained attention-based model make predictions on a massive MIMO system's channel with low-precision CSI.

This study introduces a systematic approach by integrating topological spaces with extended structures, enabling the unification of diverse semantic interpretations for modal logic within a single framework. The proposed method builds upon and expands previous theories that merged spatial and algebraic modal logic semantics. By adopting a more general concept of topological categories, the findings demonstrate that higher-order sheaves and continuous functions can be effectively represented as a type of topological category. Furthermore, the study examines how this expanded theory relates to the traditional one based on topological spaces, and explores how the main logical properties of modal logic behave when transitioning from general topological categories to the more specific case of topological spaces.

The strong edge-coloring conjecture proposed by Vizing in 1990 asserts that a strong edge-coloring exists for any bipartite graph with $ \Delta $ degrees, requiring at least $ 2\Delta - 1 $ colors. This conjecture has been verified and that a strong edge-coloring exists that uses at most $ 2\Delta - 2 $ colors in the case of bipartite graphs with maximum degree 4. In this study, we successfully construct a strong edge-coloring that uses at most 10 colors in the case of bipartite graphs with maximum degree 5. Additionally, we present colorings that use 11 and 13 colors respectively, and we extend our approach to bipartite graphs with maximum degree 6, achieving a strong edge-coloring that uses at most 13 colors. We also show that these colorings can be reduced to 12 colors in the case of bipartite graphs with maximum degree 6.

The minimal support size for a function within an eigenspace of the Hamming graph is determined. This depends on the eigenvalue index, the field characteristic, and the base of the graph. When the eigenvalue index is less than or equal to four, or the graph's base is prime, the minimal support size is exactly the eigenvalue index. However, under other conditions, the minimal support size can vary. These findings build upon previous research constraints.

This report details how to develop a web interface that interacts with the COPASI simulation engine using Python, enabling users to showcase and engage with complex systems dynamics models seen in the standalone COPASI software, now integrated with an existing R package interface. We aim to extend this functionality to a user-friendly interface using PyQT5 and web technologies, providing a seamless user experience.

Deep neural networks have emerged as a versatile tool for addressing intricate scientific problems, particularly in inverse solutions and solutions to partial differential equations. This work extends these applications to a broad class of linear operators, for which we develop a method to determine both a solution and an optimal least-squares residue when an exact match is not achievable. We also propose a novel loss function for consistently achieving this optimal residue. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through several examples, including deconvolution and tomographic imaging.

We investigate the algebra $\mathcal{Z}(C^*(\mathbb{G}))$ of classical functions on a quantum group $\mathbb{G}$ whose reduced C*-algebra is the free group C*-algebra on two generators, considering it as a subalgebra of the C*-algebra $C^*(\mathbb{G})$. Our goal is to identify the specific properties of $\mathcal{Z}(\mathbb{G})$ and the resulting quantum group $\mathbb{G}$ when this set of functions forms a maximal abelian self-adjoint subalgebra (MASA). Our analysis primarily focuses on noncompact cases, with a separate examination of the MASA properties for SU_q(2) for any real q not equal to 0. Additionally, we look at U_q(1) as another key example.

Traditional dynamic programming approaches for Markov decision processes (MDPs) often struggle due to their reliance on exhaustive state-space exploration. As MDPs get larger, their associated linear systems become ill-conditioned, making numerical methods like GMRES slower. In contrast, finite-state MDPs allow for the efficient application of value iteration and policy iteration. This is because the transition matrices in these MDPs have low ranks. In contrast, real-world large-scale MDPs or infinite MDPs like those using continuous state and action spaces have MDS matrices of full rank. This limits the traditional reinforcement learning algorithms. To address this, a new approach is proposed: approximating the MDP's transition matrix with a low-rank matrix. This enables a comparison of several policy improvement algorithms for large MDPs solved by linear programming. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration is shown to be 300 times faster than traditional policy iteration in a 10,000-state MDP. The exact linear programming value iteration is found to be the slowest, while inexact Bellman relaxation falls somewhere in the middle. These findings suggest a unifying framework for the reinforcement learning algorithms. This includes a core value function update step accelerated by inexact Newton methods. Several MDPs are used to test and compare the proposed algorithms.

For oriented graphs of degree two, we establish a theorem stating that the $k$-th symbolic power of an edge ideal in a polynomial ring equals the $k$-th ordinary power of that same ideal, where $k$ is a positive integer, under specific conditions. This result provides the first instance of a non-Borel-Sperner saturated divisorial monoid, representing an important exception to the established theory of symbolic and ordinary powers of edge ideals in oriented graphs.

To facilitate the process of calibrating a computer model, we introduce a novel approach that involves optimizing the entries of its parameter vector. This is achieved through a numerical method that maximizes or minimizes a objective function, depending on the data obtained from a experiment. The calibration process can be streamlined by leveraging the knowledge of the Jacobian of the first order, which maps the first derivative of the first component of the parameter vector to the parameter vector itself. By optimizing the entry of the parameter vector that corresponds to the objective function, a optimal step can be taken to reach a optimal solution. The proposed method is illustrated with two numerical experiments that involve the solution of an inverse problem.

This research delves into distribution-free robust learning within the framework of metric spaces. It examines the impact of concept class and query radius (a parameter representing the range of examples that must be correctly classified) on the feasibility of distribution-free robust learning. Findings reveal that distribution-free robust learning may be achievable even when the concept lacks this property, but becomes unfeasible when the query radius is restricted. Assumptions regarding the parameterized metric space and finite metric spaces yield varying outcomes, with our analysis providing novel insights into robust learning's boundaries. Our work also introduces new technical approaches and methodologies.

The presence of an isolated photon in conjunction with a jet significantly constrains the parton's virtuality at the onset of production, thereby influencing factors such as transverse momentum, $p_T$, and parton distribution functions, which in turn affects the outcome. Building upon the success of the Jet veto and the associated resummation of large logarithms of the ratio of transverse momentum to photon energy, $p_T/E_\gamma$, we extend this concept by examining the scaling behavior at very small values of $p_T/E_\gamma$. Furthermore, we apply next-to-leading order evolution to both the photon and the jet initial conditions, taking into account evolution over varying scales.

We begin by reviewing the methods of Taniguchi and Xuryk for calculating specific values of colored multiple zeta functions at level 4, alternating at weight 2 and non-alternating at level 2. Next, we derive new representations of this weight combination for weight 8, including both alternating and non-alternating variants. Our analysis demonstrates that the cost in terms of required colored multiple zeta values differs between alternating and non-alternating series, with the non-alternating series needing only 2-level values and the alternating series needing values up to level 3, specifically type (2,2,2).

The primary goal of this project is to gather accurate measurements of the W33A brown dwarf's spectrum, radial velocity, and Doppler tomography, as well as obtain precise orbital data for W33AD1 and W33AD2 through astrometric measurements and spectral analysis. These measurements, along with a detailed simulation of the brown dwarf's W33A W160 band spectrum using the WASPPO model, may help uncover new information about its system's age, assuming its luminosity and effective temperature are also known. Ultimately, achieving this goal requires obtaining high-quality W33A W160 band images and measuring its parallax, potentially using the JWST.

Our research involves a comparative analysis of an empirical model and High Energy Nuclear Collision data across different scales. The model can be adjusted to various systems and predicts specific patterns in particle production and quark yields present in High Energy Nuclear Collision data. The results also show increasing particle interactions with a decrease in the system size, transitioning from smaller to larger systems. The model is consistent with High Energy Nuclear Collision data up to a certain point, beyond which it fails to accurately predict particle production in very large systems such as those with lead ions. The model also considers the concept of "domain length," a measure of interaction range, and demonstrates a significant increase in domain length as the system size increases. The domain length is estimated to have values of around 5-7 femtometers in smaller systems but expands to over 10 femtometers in larger systems, indicating the need for potential adjustments to the model to better understand High Energy Nuclear Collision data in such cases.

Process calculations that involve the interaction of multiple particles from different hadrons require the use of double parton distribution functions, which account for the simultaneous presence of two particles within a single hadron. This paper revisits certain aspects of single and double parton distribution functions, highlighting the various constraints that they must satisfy. It also discusses evolution equations, which describe how these functions change as the momentum transfer increases. Specific DPD models that comply with the established rules of QCD are then presented in detail.

This study examines the feasibility of producing Martian and Lunar regolith materials through electrolysis to support extraterrestrial construction and in-situ manufacturing. Through laboratory simulations of eLysis on Martian and Lunar regolith, we investigated the co-electrolysis of oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen. Our results indicate that the partial pressures of partial components in simulated Martian and Lunar atmospheres inhibit the direct decomposition of carbon dioxide, but promote water decomposition and carbon deposition. Consequently, these water-splitting processes could enable the creation of engineered regolith materials, which, if further combined with in-situ methane synthesis, could support the development of valuable materials like ceramics, cements, and concrete for extraterrestrial habitats.

The behaviour of a liquid film on a fibre within a narrow channel is examined through a theoretical and numerical study. This study focuses on how slip conditions affect the liquid film, particularly in relation to shear stress differences between the fibre and the channel walls. It is found that when the fibre has lower shear stress, liquid drops form and vapor pockets develop, with drop positions influenced by slip parameters. However, when the fibre has higher shear stress, liquid drops merge into a continuous film, with shape dependent on slip conditions. This study also reveals two regimes, with distinct liquid drop configurations, arising under specific slip conditions on both the fibre and channel walls.

The recent development of the Prospector Bayesian inference framework enables precise determination of star formation rates (SFRs) from photometry and low-resolution spectra, accompanied by associated uncertainties. However, the accuracy of these SFRs is not explicitly quantified. In this study, a novel approach is introduced - the Bayesian inference of a SFR accuracy metric known as $\mathcal{L}_{\rm \beta}$ (or Br$\beta$ luminosity), a well-known proxy for SFRs, is used to further investigate Prospector's performance. Two tests are conducted to evaluate Prospector's capabilities; firstly, an analysis based on synthetic data mimicking low-resolution spectra is presented, and in this case $\mathcal{L}_{\rm \beta}$ is found to be a reliable indicator of SFR accuracy. Secondly, a demonstration based on real spectra is provided, and in this context $\mathcal{L}_{\rm \beta}$ is identified to be a strong proxy for SFRs derived from Prospector.

We develop quantum field theoretical tools to analyze key properties of 3d quantum field theories, applying the approach to compute properties of 3d N=4 orbifolds. Our findings reveal an unanticipated link between quadratic categories and exceptional braided auto-equivalences of these orbifolds. Additionally, we derive precise formulas for the 3d quantum field theories of gauge theories and observe that their supersymmetric indices conform to a specific, predicted rule.

We examine the Fisher-KPP equation in one dimension, given by $u_t = \Delta u + u(1-u)$, where the initial condition $0\leq u_0\leq 1$ is non-decreasing in the spatial variable $x$ and strictly positive and bounded within the interval $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$. By leveraging dynamic arguments and carefully constructed supersolutions and subsolutions, we derive precise asymptotic bounds for the temporal evolution of the solution $u(t,x)$ as $t$ approaches infinity and the spatial profile $u(t,x)$ as $x$ varies across all real numbers. These arguments also yield information regarding the regularity and smoothness of the solution $u(t,x)$.

This paper details our team's approach for the UbiComp 2021 Challenge in the UbiFit2021 UMBIAFUSE framework. The objective was to classify written letters utilizing temporal data gathered from a few strategically placed sensors. Our unit was positioned around a participant's hand, placing it within close proximity. We utilized an acceleration and gyroscope time series to identify written activity. This involved training a Deep Learning model on initial seconds of data, which was then evaluated using metrics to measure its accuracy. To minimize interference, we developed a filter to remove the impact of hand movements that didn't involve writing. Our method achieved a high accuracy of 95.7% in our benchmark tests.

The paper presents a novel approach to duration modeling, distinct from traditional methods that assume pre-selected distribution types. This method's flexibility enables it to discover various distribution forms for different sets of duration variables. It involves a novel regression technique and a network-based approach to model the multi-dimensional joint distribution of durations, which may be influenced by a set of determining factors. Experimental results using synthetic and real data confirm that the method effectively recovers the distribution type of durations and their conditional dispersions when durations are conditioned on a set of relevant determining factors.

Occupency modeling, a widely used statistical method for estimating ecological habitat use, benefits significantly from enhanced Bayesian approaches. Recent research integrated spatial information into this framework, but often at the cost of computational efficiency. Our work builds on this integration, developing a more computationally feasible model by combining Bayesian principles with spatial data. To this end, we merge spatially explicit spatial models with the standard occupancy framework. Our novel model incorporates a Gaussian Markov Random Field to account for spatial dependencies, enabling a Bayesian framework for quantifying ecological habitat use with spatial context. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing spatial models in terms of estimation accuracy and precision. Furthermore, our model surpasses non-spatial occupancy models when habitat distribution is spatially clustered, while providing comparable results when quantifying habitat occupancy in isolated areas. By enhancing computational efficiency and accuracy, our Bayesian framework for quantifying habitat use with spatial context can improve ecological modeling and modeling inference.

This paper introduces the Skincare project, a collaborative venture between computational intelligence, digital health, and medical experts, including general practitioners and skin disease specialists. The project's objective is to establish an advanced AI system for accurate and efficient skin disease detection and treatment recommendation. By integrating the knowledge of healthcare professionals with deep learning and transferable neural networks, the Skincare project seeks to support and expand the capabilities of medical staff. In the initial phase, the project focuses on developing a state-of-the-art diagnostic tool assisted by a supportive decision-making system.

We present a novel, generative model for sub-Gaussian distributions with pairwise correlations, and apply it to predict type Ia supernovae uncertainties. The model, characterized by its simplicity and non-parametric nature, effectively captures the full covariance structure with reduced parameters. By training a variational autoencoder with a correlation penalty, the model's latent space moves closer to the standard multivariate normal distribution. Our experimentally validated model, utilizing 148 main-sequence standard stars as reference, demonstrates the benefits of the correlation penalty in improving predictions. The updated model, named CosmoAE, shows enhanced likelihood ratios over existing types, with the potential to optimize its performance through future data collection.

Observations of the galaxy NGC 4434, an example of a merging galaxy or galaxy with galaxies interacting, have been conducted using the ALMA, VLA, and HST instruments at offset points from its center, all aligned with its direction of merger. Our observations revealed star formation occurring at the points where we observed, our analysis showed a significant mass outflow of neutral gas at a rate ten times higher than the rate of star formation occurring, 2000 M/sun/year, all of which is falling back onto the galaxy at a rate nearly ten times higher than the outflow rate, 15,000 M/sun/year at observation points with star formation occurring nearby, these rates represent ten to a hundred times higher than the rates expected in galaxies not experiencing merging or outflows. Further analysis revealed that at observation points with no star formation occurring the neutral gas outflow and infall rates are relatively low compared to observation points with star formation occurring significantly, these rates were estimated at a rate of about 10 percent of those observed at observation points with star formation occurring significantly, these rates have implications for how we understand the process of quenching in galaxies due to how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how we have observed that how

The interaction of particle-laden plumes with fluid environments was investigated through numerical simulations. These simulations focused on plumes initialized with a constant combination of flow and particle mass excess, where particle sedimentation leads to increased entrainment of fluids when the plume's buoyancy flow is directed opposite to the particles' buoyancy. This increased entrainment is attributed to the particle sedimentation triggering flow collapse and instability. In contrast, when the plumes initialized with constant particle mass excess, decreased entrainment was observed. These results are analyzed using the plumes' three-dimensional dynamics, revealing that significant particle sedimentation along the plume's forward path leads to enhanced collapse and increased entrainment of fluids.

In general graph-based models of contagion, where vertices represent individuals and edges represent interactions, the assumption is made that an infected individual has a constant probability of transmitting the disease to any connected infected-free individual. Our model generalizes this to hypergraphs, where groups of individuals can interact simultaneously, to which our model can apply, in which an infected vertex has a certain probability of transmitting the disease to any related infected-free vertex. The model's infection rate is influenced by the size of the transmitted groups. The maximum possible infection rate is determined, and this is related to the concept of hypergraph density. A polynomial-time algorithm is proposed to compute this value.

By experimentally manipulating the crystal structure of a Fe/FeRh ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic bilayer system, researchers have achieved an anti-persistent spin texture with high degrees of control. The findings show that compressive strain transforms the interface antiferromagnetic coupling into a mechanism that induces blocking and eliminates the inhomogeneous spin texture, effectively offering a strain-based method to switch between controllable antiferromagnetic and magnetically soft states. This discovery highlights the importance of crystal structure in shaping magnetic properties that can influence next-generation spintronic technologies.

Our study demonstrates, through three-dimensional global magnetohydrodynamic simulations, that the behavior of magnetic dynamos in faster-rotating stars can provide key insights into the occurrence of magnetic cycles in slower-rotation stars. Specifically, we found that the dynamo mechanism employed in these stars is capable of producing magnetic cycles even in stars with very slow rotation, which is typically associated with the occurrence of such cycles. The simulated magnetic cycles are characterized by a mean cycle length of approximately 27 years, which is comparable to the observed length of solar cycles. Additionally, the cycle strength exhibits a peak in activity during periods of higher rotation, which is consistent with observations of certain stars. Moreover, our model can accurately reproduce established solar and stellar observation patterns, which is achieved by accurately capturing the differential rotation of the stars and employing a dynamo mechanism that is in line with observed features of solar and stellar magnetism.

We introduce a model that learns multiple outputs from multiple inputs by sharing a common hidden layer. The proposed model enhances the efficiency of neural networks by reducing the number of parameters needed and improving its ability to capture common input patterns for distinct outputs. Initially, we explore a straightforward application of the model on simple regression tasks with multiple outputs to demonstrate its benefits. Subsequently, we refine the model to address more complex scenarios, including scenario-dependent hidden states and input-conditional hidden states. Through rigorous testing on several datasets, we show that the proposed model significantly outperforms existing models in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

mc-ATM is a case study used to test and demonstrate the capabilities of mcMini, an innovative model checker designed for verifying multi-threaded operations under weak memory conditions. Specifically, mc-ATM examines concurrent actions involving at least two threads, with thread 1 executing a store operation and another thread executing a load operation, both involving memory addresses. mcMini, an advanced implementation based on the Engleherd et al. framework, outperforms many model checkers in handling complex memory scenarios, particularly when dealing with operations that can be reordered by the system. Additionally, mcMini includes an optimized version for accelerating model checking processes, an effective method for reducing the state space to avoid redundant computations, and supports concurrency oracles for filtering out unrealistic execution paths, such as those that are temporally impossible or involve unfair scheduling of threads.

Recently, Facebook's WhatsApp has implemented new features to mitigate the spread of misinformation in its instant messaging platform. Although this initiative aims to address a significant concern, the platform's design and management continue to raise questions about the effectiveness of mitigation efforts in curbing the spread of false information online. This study investigates Instagram's image-based misinformation campaigns in Brazil and how WhatsApp facilitates the spread of such content, based on users' interactions with shared media. Our findings reveal that WhatsApp users are more inclined to engage with media posts, thereby amplifying the reach and impact of such posts, even without direct engagement. Consequently, our results suggest that WhatsApp's design may undermine its intended mitigation efforts and highlight the challenges in tackling the issue of online misinformation.

Our study examines how genetic mutations affect population diversity and evolves into a population model with a modifying force. The force alters the population's genetic makeup based on past configurations. To achieve this, we modify the classic Wright-Fisher model and analyze its long-term behavior. A Riemann-Hilbert problem is used to prove the existence of a unique solution that describes the population's fitness distribution. As the population size increases, our solution approximates the population's fitness distribution with a controlled error, which decreases proportionally with the parameter's inverse square root.

A novel and efficient deep learning architecture, known as DeepForest, has been developed to enhance the detection of speech artifacts in spoofing countermeasures. By incorporating an attention mechanism, DeepForest optimally extracts features from speech recordings, leading to improved performance. A fundamental forest model forms the core of Deepforest, utilizing an innovative concept to streamline model training. Furthermore, an innovative strategy was introduced to utilize authentic replayed voices as supplementary data during training, resulting in significant gains for both the individual basic models and the integrated Deepforest system. Comprehensive evaluations using benchmark datasets demonstrate that Deepforest consistently achieves superior accuracy in artifact detection compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

We begin with a supergravity theory, establishing links to both low-energy effective fields and quantum gravity. The field is divided into distinct sectors, each with its own self-contained interactions. Focusing on the K\"ahler and hypermultiplet sectors, we derive the geometry of their respective manifolds. The hypermultiplet manifold, when a certain condition is met, forms a specific type of fibred manifold, with the base determined by a superpotential related to a holomorphic prepotential on the axidilaton manifold. A complex to conformal supergravity, we first build a frame for a top-down supergravity theory and then obtain an CFT through a fibre Weyl symmetry. The resulting theory involves a superconformal manifold on the hypermultiplet sector, with a $SU(2)_R$ fibering over a complex manifold. The $SU(2)_R$ is dual to the U(1) manifold, forming the basis of the CFT. The axidilaton superpotential on this dual manifold is related to a Fermi manifold prepotential, with the hypermultiplet sector being a Fermi manifold, from which we calculate the Fermi manifold's prepotential. The axidilaton dilaton, reflecting the CFT's central charge, gives a lower bound on the central charge, with the lower bound dependent on the fibre genus. The lower bound is also reflected in the superpotential upper bound on the fibering complex manifold. The method is

The effect of reversing the pump propagation direction in a silicon microdisk is examined by analyzing the coherence functions of four-wave mixed photon pairs. The change in coherence functions upon reversing the pump direction reveals information about the spatial and temporal properties of the mode field. The findings also demonstrate that the coherence of the emitted photons can be adjusted by selecting specific pump travel paths.

This study investigates electrical characteristics in two types of silicon surface oxide structures, comparing traditional Si SOS with enhanced Si ESOS. It is discovered that the latter exhibits superior quality, exhibiting a $10^{11}$ cm$^{-2}$ carrier concentration, $10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$ trap density, and $10^{9}$ eV cm$^{-3}$ fixed charge. Notably, the surface potential within the etched region approaches thermal equilibrium. Furthermore, the ESOS surface demonstrates minimal changes in carrier concentration following high temperature processing.

For any $n \in \mathbb{N}$ or $\omega$, if partitioning the real line into $n$ Borel sets requires a specific cardinality, it also requires that many for $n$ closed sets. Furthermore, for any infinite cardinal $\alpha$, the real line can be divided into $\alpha$ closed sets with a specific topological properties, but even $\alpha+1$ Borel sets with a similar properties, in the same topology, cannot have this properties.

This paper delves into the concept of short-term reversal trading and its linked strategies, such as commodity trading. We successfully create a computational model to simulate short-term reversal traders and demonstrate that a cooperative relationship between them and commodity trading advisors (CTAs) can be mutually beneficial. Conversely, non-CTA short-term reversal traders ultimately suffer financially. Furthermore, our study reveals that CTA firms that engage in short-term reversal trading and those that do not but profit from its external effects can both thrive.

This research explores how current Dynamic Protocol Detection mechanisms, used in network monitoring tools, can be bypassed by malicious attacks. Such mechanisms, based on active testing, help identify abnormal protocols but can be deceived by attacks that exploit their limitations. Attacks that respond to probing packets in real-time are extremely difficult to detect, posing a threat to system security. Our study focuses on the data-driven DPD approach, using machine learning to improve detection accuracy. By collecting and analyzing data from various applications, including normal and abnormal protocols, we trained multiple classification models. Our findings, through evaluation metrics, reveal the effectiveness of these evasion attacks, as well as the potential improvements in evasion difficulty, especially with hyperparameter tuning. Our open-source code, using the Sketeh protocol, provides valuable insights into the potential vulnerabilities of current DPD mechanisms, thereby highlighting areas for enhancement.

When a magnetic film comes into contact with a superconducting strip, an interaction arises leading to the coexistence of magnons and superconducting pairs. Initially appearing as an attractive force, this interaction evolves into a repulsive one as the magnetic field strength increases, ultimately causing the on-shell T-matrix to diverge at a specific point. Near this critical field, the leading behavior is accurately described by an enhanced exchange interaction. Furthermore, the presence of the superconducting strips introduces scattering centers for magnons, resulting in the formation of magnonic interference patterns, standing waves, and localized states within the magnetic film.

Recent advances in federated learning have primarily focused on protecting user data, but a potential issue with the FL approach is that the model may change significantly after each interaction, leading to poor performance on different datasets. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, practical framework that combines the benefits of both transfer learning and FL. Our framework utilizes domain adaptation over the transferred model to ensure it performs well on various datasets, without incurring the additional costs. Our theoretical analysis shows that the FL approach without our proposed method risks producing poor results, whereas, using our proposed approach yields satisfactory results. Our proposed framework was experimentally verified on different synthetic and real-world datasets and it showcases improved performance.

A crucial tool in quantum information processing and computation is the quantum Fourier transform. This article presents newly developed quantum gates applicable to high-dimensional multi-photon systems used in quantum communication. The proposed circuit uses a multi-photon system as its foundation. The transform's application enables access to richer information within each qubit of these systems. The article demonstrates these doors using photonic qubits in orbital angular momentum and shows how they can be applied to quantum computing and the quantum internet.

In a hybrid analog-digital reception system with increasing numbers of antennas and passive units, we compare two methods for channel channel optimization and evaluate its performance, ultimately determining the more effective method for channel optimization. Specifically, we analyze a setup with a single passive unit, a known phase shift pattern, and analyze the performance of maximum likelihood and other optimization-based methods in channel channel optimization. We then extend our analysis to a multi-antenna setup with multiple antennas at the receiver.

This research examined the COVID-19 related content within Indiana newspapers, both online and in print, between March 1, 2020, and April 30, 2020. By utilizing online database searches and data from the Indiana Yearbook, we examined 176,614 articles and found that local news coverage peaked on March 29 at 1,319 articles per day. The results indicated that state, federal, and health-related sources, such as the CDC and WHO, were primary influences on content. Notably, news about the virus and its health implications dominated early coverage, but stories related to non-pharmaceutical interventions and community response gained prominence in the final month. The most frequent article sources shifted from news agencies to government press releases, press release content being more likely to appear in the print edition.

The topic of counting beyond trained examples through logical inference within latent variables within neural networks has garnered significant interest within the machine learning community, nonetheless models exhibiting this ability have not been systematically identified or analyzed outside of specific academic contexts. In our research, we demonstrate that systematic extrapolation serves as a broad indicator of how neural networks learn to count through logical inference within latent variables. By examining various image-based models that were trained to count, we found that those exhibiting accurate systematic extrapolation also showed precise counts for unseen numbers, produced linearly scaling neural activations, and produced similarly scaled attention patterns. Conversely, notable exceptions to this relationship have not been found. Moreover, we have developed a new approach to utilizing transformer-based neural networks in the 101 problem that exhibits all the characteristics associated with systematic counting.

We introduce xor filters, an innovative data structure that serves as a swift and memory-efficient alternative to the renowned Bloom filter, offering false positive rates and performance consistency akin to well-designed hyperloglog blocks. Xor filters integrate elements of the Bloom filter, a technique first detailed by Burbea and Dyer in 2017, and later applied by Kirsch and Mitzenmacher in 2017. Our research involves an in-depth examination of the design and performance of xor filters, discovering that they can be constructed in a user-friendly manner and effectively combine multiple bloom filters into a single, compact data structure. Additionally, an analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of various parameters on xor filter performance. When optimally designed, xor filters outperform existing space savings filters by an order of magnitude, even outperforming advanced Bloom filter variations that utilize lazy insertion and deletion in nearly all test scenarios. Our find is that they can be built in a straightforward, intuitive manner through a step-by process. Moreover, our research indicates that they enable rapid query processing. However, it's crucial to note that xor filters are not suitable for the inclusion of duplicate elements due to the elimination of repeated bits. Nevertheless, they exhibit some degree of duplicate tolerance in the event of random input. Furthermore, a xortable filter, an extension of the xor filter that allows for sorted set membership queries, is also presented in this study. Our analysis shows that this filter outperforms other filters with comparable

This study develops an Alexandrov body construction based on the divisorial Zariski decomposition and divisorial移动, which we initially established. By leveraging Birkhoff's linear order properties of the real number system, we prove that this body is complete if and only if the underlying surface is divisorial moving. Additionally, this representation as the Alexandrov body facilitates proving that any real-bounded pseudo-metric on the surface is equivalent to a strong real metric when the surface is divisorial moving.

The level of detail in financial data varies across time scales, and understanding how to extract meaningful information from it is crucial. High-frequency data contains more complete market information but also includes noise, while lower-frequency data has less noise but also less informative content. The direction of information flow can be influenced by the time it takes to be obtained, and there is a need to determine the most effective frequency at which to use data. In this context, a unique approach is presented where the past of stock market transactions is utilized to identify the optimal time scale for current market directional information. By modeling the order flow and market maker behavior, and employing a Fourier spectral analysis, it is possible to perform an "FFT-01" that transforms order books into price variances. The resulting price data can then be used to reconstruct past price histories, and through cross-spectral analysis, it is possible to determine the lag at which past and present market information intersect. The findings from this study suggest that using a time lag of around 30 seconds provides the most effective frequency for determining market direction in the NYSE. Additionally, it was possible to reconstruct past price histories using high-frequency data and achieve a mean absolute percentage error of around 0.1%.

FLVoogd, a clustering framework, processes personal data in an error-correcting code space to prevent leaks while preserving utility. It employs a combination of techniques, including code-space distance to safeguard privacy and a weighted Ising model for enhanced clustering. By controlling these mechanisms, FLVoigt balances utility and privacy on robust data representations, effectively performing weighted Ising model clustering using the FLOVOOGD algorithm. Evaluation on synthetic and real-world data shows FLVoigt's effectiveness in producing high-quality clusters, even while preventing unnecessary misclassifications.

The 2018 Grand Challenge in autonomous vehicles highlighted an essential issue: many entries rely on simulations, raising concerns about the gap between trained models in virtual environments and their real-world applications. Research in sim2real transfer typically focuses on single domains, but the Grand Challenge entries utilized various simulation tools, implying that transfer must occur not just from simulation to reality, but also between different simulations. We investigate this multi-sim2real problem by presenting an early attempt to combine and transfer between diverse simulation environments, as well as from simulation to reality, in the context of autonomous driving. In this framework, individual simulations or the aggregate of all simulations function as distinct sources, each either offering a particular viewpoint or representing a combination of all perspectives. Our goal is to create a unified destination domain that reflects a optimal blend of these sources. By applying this concept to the 2018 Grand Challenge datasets using a framework that assesses and transfers domain adaptation error, we compare various strategies, including individual, aggregate-weighted, and similarity-based approaches to domain measurement and adaptation.

The growing sophistication of deepfake media has raised significant concerns about the potential risks it poses, leading to a vast array of research topics being explored, from technologies and tools to policies, guidelines, and laws. Despite this vast amount of research, a unified body of guidelines, policies, or laws has not emerged from it. In light of this, we aim to contribute by offering a framework for translating research into practice, along with an analysis of the current state of affairs. Our framework, rooted in the SEEP model - SEverity, EXisting practice, EXpected practice, and Prioritization - assesses each research topic from a unique perspective. In doing so, we identify areas where further exploration is required to address the gaps between existing practices and expected realities, ultimately, we provide recommendations on how to transform research into a tangible impact, all while acknowledging the complexities inherent in each priority we discuss.

The size of an Earth's atmosphere is better understood when considering a gradual process of atmospheric development. A massive initial atmosphere would be expanded by solar radiation, allowing for a more extensive composition. However, as the atmosphere evolves and develops an optical depth greater than one, it would cool down and shrink, leading to the loss of cool gases. Consequently, temperate planets with large atmospheres are expected to have lower concentrations of cool gases, such as carbon and nitrogen, in comparison to planets with smaller atmospheres, which are more similar to our own. It is also possible that local phenomena, such as lightning, could lead to the creation of an ozone layer, regardless of the atmosphere's size.

The classic Hopfield network excels at associative memory but falls short in learning new patterns due to a single bulk learning process. To address this limitation, a modified McCulloch-Pitts network was developed, a sparsely connecting Hopfield network with a fully connected input layer, enabling enhanced learning ability while maintaining the network's simplicity.

However, this modified architecture introduces new challenges, such as pattern-dependent dynamics that impede understanding and analysis, as well as the need for extensive simulations to evaluate its performance. To overcome these limitations, a theorems-based analysis was employed in conjunction with random graph theory to explore the network's dynamics.

A key finding in this research involved identifying a "pattern memory phase" characterized by stable fluctuations, which enabled the network to retain and recall previously learned patterns with high accuracy after the initial learning phase.

Moreover, it was discovered that increasing network connectivity enhances pattern retention during recall, a counterintuitive result in the context of neural networks.

Finally, extensive simulations confirmed these theoretical predictions and demonstrated the network's ability to retain and generalize new patterns.

This paper introduces OutOViL, an innovative, comprehensive, and publicly available resource for modern scene text recognition out-of-vocabulary (OOV) detection. OutOViL consists of 40 datasets representing diverse real-world environments, with a total of 112,530 images, 3,060,153 text instances, and 19,550 unique classes. By utilizing the OutOViL dataset, researchers have trained a model, with the results showing significant improvements over previous models in 11 different evaluations. Furthermore, the paper outlines strategies to enhance model performance, with potential for even more substantial advancements. OutOViL, along with the accompanying code, can be accessed at https://outovil.ai.

Isolated system solutions or "branches" can be found using a robust numerical method, especially for complex parameter-dependent systems that arise in various scientific and engineering fields. Traditionally, these solutions are computed by starting with an approximate solution and making small adjustments, often using the system's derivatives to guide the process. However, a new, reliable numerical method is presented in this research, which finds branches without using derivatives and starts with approximate solutions in the form of rational functions. This new method is particularly useful in solving systems of nonlinear equations and has many potential applications, such as studying bifurcations and solving eigenvalue problems.

Industrial applications often face the challenge of identifying system failures and detecting their occurrences using limited data. To address this, an iterative approach is proposed that enhances the performance of both change point detection and failure mode isolation methods. The proposed sequential changes to parameters enable adaptive tuning, yielding superior outcomes compared to existing approaches. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through industrial case studies. Additionally, considering the constraints of industrial settings, a user-friendly implementation is developed and can be deployed on edge devices. Specifically, the approach is implemented using efficient neural network-based models, including a novel method for failure detection and a novel method for change point detection, both of which exhibit superior performance and execution times.

The Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) dwarf galaxy exhibits two distinct velocity peaks within its stellar composition, suggesting the possible presence of a second constituent, named Wukong (initially identified as LMS-1), with unique characteristics. This second peak is quiet, slow, and located far from the supermassive black hole at the center of galaxies. Despite thorough statistical analysis and an in-depth examination of potential biases, we have determined that the underlying distribution of velocities is likely intrinsic to the system. By analyzing the system's formation through our metal content, age, and orbital properties, we have found that the GSE and Wukong components share similar star formation durations of around 2 billion years, and that their accretion occurred at different times, around 5 and 3 gigayears ago, respectively. Although some researchers have interpreted the velocity peaks as signs of distinct merger events, we have developed an alternative explanation where the secondary component's velocity peak is eliminated due to the eroding effect of the giant black hole on its orbits.

For an excellent, strongly $0$-dimensional, torsion-free pro-finite group $\Gamma$ with a surjective map to a pro-p group, and a torsion-free ring spectrum $Z$, we establish the existence of a canonical equivalence from the homotopy orbit spectrum of $Z[[\Gamma]]$ to $Z$ under the conditions that its homotopy coins are equivalent to a sphere. This holds particularly when the formality of $Z[[\Gamma]]$ matches the formality of $Z$.

Acquiring labeled data can be costly and time-consuming, yet it's essential for training machine learning models. Selective labeling, a process of labeling only certain data, can reduce annotation costs, but it also risks model performance if the labeling criteria are inappropriate. This work proposes a novel algorithm that labels data based on its similarity to target class prototypes, ensuring that labeled data is representative of underlying data distributions. Due to robustness against label noise, this method uses data prototypes derived from clean labels, and can be integrated with learning algorithms, such as K-means, for further enhancement. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that this method consistently outperforms existing labeling approaches, providing an effective solution for acquiring labeling-efficient data.

A even-odd anomaly observed in magnetoresistance measurements of lateral spin valves indicates electronic dispersed states at the InAs valence band maximum. These dispersed states are believed to arise from valence band manipulation and possibly other electronic contributions such as charge transfer from spin polarized EuS to InAs. Furthermore, the team found that magnetization direction within the EU/IS spin valve exhibits an unusual in-plane orientation, deviating from the typical perpendicular magnetization direction typically seen in such structures.

We demonstrate that the interactiveness of a computer influences its ability to resolve certain mathematical challenges reminiscent of oracle-models issues, despite these challenges being solvable within the context of second-order arithmetic. Specifically, the determinism and ordinal analysis of a computer depends on its physical traits, akin to models-constructed via forced expansion, but with a key difference: a more powerful computer can create models where the determinism and analysis of less powerful machines are invalid.

Neural network models have become increasingly complex, but their size and computation requirements can be particularly challenging for computer vision applications. Reducing the computational efficiency of these models, especially for vision tasks, is a pressing concern. Various techniques such as pruning, quantization, and hardware design have been proposed, but each comes with potential downsides like performance degradation or increased computational costs. To address this issue, ClickTrain is presented, a method for identifying critical connections in models and reducing the computational load more effectively. ClickTrain operates by pinpointing high-value components in a model, similar to a training process, and shrinking them with minimal performance impact. ClickTrain enables aggressive model compression with higher compared to previous pruning methods. Additionally, ClickTrain can optimize any model by merging its parts. Experiments on various face recognition tasks with state-of-the-art models demonstrate the efficiency and flexibility of ClickTrain.

This study presents a framework for interpreting substructural modal logics by extending the four-valued semantics developed by Bumm and Smolka. Building upon this foundation, we derive a corresponding semantics for basic logic and a corresponding one for linear logic. By adopting a general framework, we establish a comprehensive semantics for multiple modalities of each logic. This comprehensive interpretation yields an original and complete modalization of both the basic and linear logic. Furthermore, we show the ability to embed any modal logic based on the basic or linear logic into the respective higher-order logic, thus demonstrating a connections between these formal systems.

TOI-5542, the most recent addition to the TESS view, is an M4 dwarf with a mass of 0.343 M$_\odot$, a radius of 0.33 R$_\odot$, and a temperature of 3382 K, located 24.12 parsecs away. The M4 dwarf TOI-5542 has one confirmed planet, TOI-5542 b, discovered by TESS Planets, with a unique star-to-planet distance of 0.04815 astronomical units. A strong indication of atmospheric moisture exists in the exoplanet TOI-5542 b, and a global temperature of 288 K, equivalent to Earth's, can be found in its atmosphere. The volume of this planet is approximately 2.37 times that of Earth, and a formation scenario of gas-enveloped terrestrial planets is proposed for TOI-5542 b, with a core mass potentially as high as 1.97 times that of Earth. The findings from this study highlight the significance of TOI-5542 b in the study of planetary composition and formation.

This study proposes a sampling-based primal-dual algorithm to rapidly find a useful starting solution and enhance operational policies in large-scale complex problems. A specific example of such a problem is the management of resources to prevent disruptions from having a major impact. The method uses randomization and relies on the duality theory, but it often ends up solving unmanageably large mathematical models due to the details it incorporates. We address these limitations by applying the algorithm to solve an online problem of matching pairs at a major sporting event. A key feature of our approach is its ability to continuously refine an upper and lower bound on optimal policy values, allowing it to create better decision rules within a reasonable time frame. We demonstrate that using the algorithm to generate more accurate operational policies can significantly improve the efficiency of event management systems, ultimately leading to major policy decisions being made faster.

This research introduces a novel mathematical symbol recognition framework that incorporates subgraph matching and adjacency label information. We begin by decomposing a mathematical symbol into nodes and edges. Then, node recognition is carried out using graph-based segmentation, while subgraph-based adjacent edge recognition is performed with a kNN classifier to incorporate adjacency information. After testing on the OCR-Sym dataset, our method demonstrates a significant 10.4% increase in recognition accuracy compared to the existing graph-based approach, by adding minimal 3% computational overhead.

BPS states that arise from sheaves on the Hilbert scheme of $K$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$
form the basis for understanding the growth of instanton sectors in 3d $\mathcal{N}=4$
vector multiplets. Utilizing "plethystic logarithms", we analyze how the size
of these sectors increases with $K$ and derive an approximate formula for their
growth rate. This discovery also yields insights into the growth of instanton sectors
in related 5d $\mathcal{N}=1$ theories. Additionally, we identify potential
implications for understanding wall-crossing and conjectures by Bezrukavnikov,
Ivanov, and Odessky.

In many real-world networks, the majority of nodes are interconnected through bridges, the removal of which would significantly fragment the network. We investigate how the presence of bridges in an susceptible-infected-susceptible network impacts the predictability of epidemic spreading. We found that, given a certain threshold, the bridgeness of a network, constructed from a random directed network where the average number of connections per node is around 2.3, is comparable to that of small-world and ER models. We also discovered that, as the bridgeness increases, the ability to predict epidemic final sizes using mean-field theory decreases. Furthermore, we found that networks with high bridgeness tend to have a more structured susceptible profile. We also demonstrated that, for a certain threshold, the average degree required to make mean-field theory accurate for R0 calculation in an ESRT network is approximately 2.3, regardless of the bridgeness. We found that the mean-field theory overestimates the size of epidemics when a significant portion of the population is immune, but this discrepancy decreases when epidemics are larger and the proportion of immune nodes is smaller, particularly when the average degree is around 2.3.

In the field of reinforcement learning, researchers are increasingly interested in solving highly constrained safety problems. A major challenge in this area is striking a balance between exploring the environment to learn and adhering to safety constraints. Traditional safety constraints can be difficult to follow due to their strict nature, as even minor transgressions result in significant penalties. A minor risk of potentially necessary safety constraint violations may lead to exploration failure and hinder learning. To address this limitation, we introduce a new method that uses an auxiliary model to predict and soften safety constraints, thus allowing for a higher level of exploration. This method is implemented using the Off Policy Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithm. Our approach was tested in a 2D robot simulation environment with multiple, complex safety constraints and demonstrated improved safety and efficiency. Additionally, we propose an iterative method for learning and applying this softened constraint, enabling consideration of an ever-increasing number of safety constraints.

A new approach to identifying twin primes is presented, which is based on the idea of twin prime generators. As proven by Chen in 1993, one of the twin primes in any twin prime pair has a prime as its successor. Building on this, the author has shown that twin primes can be expressed as the product of specific numbers within a given interval n to n+2, which are each the successor of a prime or a prime themselves. It is an unproven hypothesis that the numbers a and b, in the expression (a-1)(b-1) = n(n + 1), are both located in the same interval n to n + c for some constant c. This leads to a formula for counting twin primes: T(n) = Σ(a-1)(Σb) - Σ(a-1) n(Σ(b-1)).

This research article outlines a novel, two-tiered control system designed for mobile platforms sonar-assisted navigation, incorporating an sonar-assisted guidance module and a safe navigation controller. Utilizing model predictive control, the guidance module optimizes the trajectory for minimizing sonar distance to obstacles. Implementing a maximum permissible maneuvering limit, the safe navigation controller adjusts trajectory parameters when necessary to prevent collisions. Given that mobile robots are often equipped with basic sonar arrays, our algorithm relies solely on the sonar angles to order sensors and select the furthest obstacle for predictive control. Simulation studies using a sonar setup with nine elements validate the proposed controller.

The most distinct feature of Nereid's spectrum sets it apart from other icy objects in the outer solar system. Its spectrum resembles that of (90482) 2003 FY259 and the active comet 67T/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, both of which show signs of sublimation activity and surface compositions containing organic compounds like tholins. These similarities in spectral characteristics and potential activity suggest that Nereid's surface may also contain volatile ices capable of sublimating and depositing fresh material, which could explain its heavily cratered and ancient surface.

We extend the concept of affine planes to arbitrary rings by leveraging the projective line of a ring $S$, denoted as $\mathbb{P}^1_S$. This allows us to investigate which ring homomorphisms $f\colon S\to R$ transform the projective line of $S$ into the affine plane of $R$. Furthermore, it is shown that the image of $\mathbb{P}^1_S$ in $\mathbb{P}^2_R$ via such a homomorphism can be described by specific equations. Building on this foundation, we explore how these results apply to the study of Bruhat--Tits buildings associated with general linear groups, specifically the pair $(\mathbf{PGL}_n,R)$, where a map $(\mathbf{PGL}_n,S)\to (\mathbf{PGL}_n,R)$ is considered.

The introduction of models, cardinalities, and cardinalities in the real line via transfinite induction on the constructible universe helps in understanding implications between various features of the cardinals in the most conservative manner possible. By analyzing the impact of adding new real numbers to existing models on the real line, we can determine specific characteristics such as the size of the set of all real numbers. Specifically, we can establish relationships between the size of the set of all real numbers, the size of the set of all real numbers that are not in the model, and the effectiveness of certain forcing methods in preserving non-constructible real numbers.

We integrate the well-known pessimism principle with Thompson sampling (P-Sampling) and show its efficacy in both dynamic treatment optimization and multi-armed bandit problems with a dependent setting. P-Sampling can be interpreted as a form of optimistic pessimism and offers a straightforward alternative to both Optimistic Optimism and Optimistic Pessimism while also being easier to implement. Furthermore, Optimistic Pessimism is found to be an optimistic version of Thompson Sampling. We establish that the P-Sampling policy achieves a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{KT\log^{2}K})$ and also present experimental results that validate its effectiveness.

We hold that certain subcategories of finitely defined modules over noetherian rings, which are capable of fully discerning these modules, remain stable under the action of derived equivalent rings. This finding reinforces and broadens the existing variance invariance of finitely generated modules within the framework of derived equivalences. As a direct consequence, it is established that the higher algebraic K-groups associated with such rings, expressed in terms of the full subcategories, exhibit invariance under the said equivalences.

A method is proposed to connect various quantum configurations through simulations, creating a hierarchical structure among them. This framework enables the gradual transition from lower levels of quantum behavior, such as nonlocality, to higher levels, such as contextuality, as described by various polytopes. The method also facilitates a step-by-step increase in the complexity of these higher-level behaviors, consistent with the nested nature of these polytopes. This approach provides a unified understanding of different hierarchical behaviors, similar to how existing research has stepped from Bell nonlocality to coarse-grained Bell nonlocality. Additionally, the method allows for the creation of novel, nontrivial examples of contextuality and nonlocality through a progressive construction process. It serves as an illustrative tool for developing original theoretical examples in the field.

In multi-band Hubbard models with exact η-pairing ground states, the strongest pairing, as measured by complex correlation functions, occurs at half-filling. We establish this phenomenon for a broad class of multi-orbital systems, including those where all orbitals experience η-pairing, as well as more general cases with multiple orbital degeneracies. For multi-orbital systems, the required conditions are minimal, allowing for a more widespread applicability of η-pairing. However, in cases with a single orbital but multiple degeneracies, η-pairing cannot hold due to the presence of high-energy virtual states. For model Hamiltonians that respect lattice symmetry, the strongest pairing, however, still occurs at half-filling, consistent with results from theoretical analyses and a similar effect observed in the Gutzwiller variational framework. The underlying mechanism responsible for this pairing behavior is the suppression of virtual hopping between filled and empty states. Additionally, a novel form of pairing is identified, encompassing correlation functions with an odd number of gamma factors. This pairing, while not strictly adhering to η-pairing, exhibits similarities and results in the strongest occurrence at half-filling. The findings hold considerable relevance for understanding physical systems, including those with near-degenerate orbital energies. The results may also hold for more general model Hamiltonians, such as the general one-band model.
