This work addresses the generalized Polya theorem for a-adic solenoids. We consider an a-adic solenoid T and a function fa-1: I to T such that fa-1(x+a-1)=a fa-1(x). Our results include an expression for all functions fa-1: I to T in terms of continuous functions from I to T, as well as an investigation into the space of such functions with specific topological properties.

Organisations with a network of geographically dispersed sensors can gather vast amounts of data on the distribution of organisms, including rare and invasive species. This large dataset, containing information from various locations, can be analysed to create predictive models and visualize spatial patterns. Furthermore, data from these sensors can be organised into distinct species-rich communities based on species presence, similar to how existing data has been clustered into distinct biomes. Present methods to perform this clustering either rely on the researcher to pre-define the number of communities or assume all species have an equal importance. In contrast, a new approach is introduced that automatically determines the appropriate number of clusters and differentiates between species based on their frequency of occurrence by adapting an existing method known as Dirichlet Process Mixture Models. This modified method removes assumptions about commonalities in the probability of species presence across the network of sensors and utilizes a dynamic process to identify the best clusters. In doing so, it identifies key generalist and specialist species present in each community, as well as their respective frequencies. Furthermore, this new method can be applied not only to species presence-absence data, but also to abundance data, as demonstrated through simulation studies and real-world examples of beetle distribution in New York City's Central Park.

Salient object detection, a fundamental computer vision task, focuses on identifying the most noticeable objects within an image. Recent advancements have explored multi-task learning approaches that combine RGB and RGB-D images to leverage depth data and enhance performance, particularly in RGB-D images. However, existing methods typically process these inputs separately, leading to unnecessary computational costs when dealing with RGB images. We introduce a novel framework processing RGB and RGB-D features within a unified structure, allowing simultaneous network sharing for both types of inputs, significantly reducing computational load, especially in RGB images. Furthermore, our method employs a novel depth metric learning approach, leveraging contrastive learning with virtual positive and negative samples to maximize performance on RGB and RGB-D images. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving superior performance on salient object detection in RGB and RGB-D images, while also gaining a 40% processing speed increase in RGB images.

This paper outlines abuse detection in English tweets using an open challenge that was part of the 2021 Discourse Forum. Our approach involved analyzing the semantic content of tweets in a model that also considered associated user profile information. The primary task focused on identifying abusive content, for which we submitted a system achieving a macro F1 score of 0.7611. A complementary task explored the identification of abusive content types in tweets, and our model for this achieved an macro F1 score of 0.4411.

I offer a proof that the set of integers in base $b$ that do not contain a specific substring as a contiguous sequence of digits, but only as a palindromic sequence, has a limit that can be expressed as $\lambda_{\text{pal}}(b)$ with $0<\lambda_{\text{pal}}(b)<1$. This result applies to any base $b\geq 2$ and demonstrates, in particular, that the set of integers in base $b$ that never contain a run of $2$ has a positive density, addressing a question by Akiyama, van Liere, and Salo.

We introduce a novel unsupervised image reconstruction method that can effectively handle various types of noise, including Poisson, Gaussian, and more complex distributions, in CT images. The method utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network and a new loss function that encourages the model to learn robust noise and image features, thereby improving image quality and fidelity. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through CT image reconstruction experiments, showing its ability to accelerate data acquisition and enhance the overall image quality.

This work leverages Bayesian Program Learning to encode handwritten text as a probabilistic sequence of symbolic elements. By applying synthetic data augmentation and leveraging an implicit continuous-to-discrete prior, our approach enables generation of highly realistic handwriting variations from the smallest possible sample sizes. This is possible because our model captures the joint distribution between sample handwrites and their underlying syntactic structures. Consequently, when producing handwrites from any grammatically correct sentence structure, a diverse and coherent style is automatically inferred. Furthermore, due to the compactness of BPL's grammatical representations, converting them into visual forms is an efficient process. This enables sampling at the character or word level, resulting in style-consistent but syntactically varied generated handwrites. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the scalability and generative capabilities of our approach, which outperforms previous methods in producing realistic handwritten text.

A new approach is presented for the systematic generation of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements based on effective field theory principles. Unlike previous methods limited to specific bases or 3-body states, this approach can be applied to any basis or 3-nucleon state and leverages modern computing techniques. To demonstrate its efficiency, matrix elements from the $V_{low-k}$ potential are calculated and validated using the AV18 potential as a reference. The findings show that the revised storage method significantly reduces memory needs to around 10 MB and that an 8 CPU system can be optimized to nearly double its speed by intelligently reusing memory.

Quantum electronic phenomena are explored using two primary methods: the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix method. To effectively understand quantum electronic behavior, it's essential to apply modern many-body Green-function theory. The paper emphasizes the group structure in quantum electronics and approximates the entanglement between electrons and fields based on the separation of quantum electronic and quantum electrodynamics components within the total wave function.

Let's consider a subset $\Omega$ in complex n-dimensional space that is both bounded and convex. The space is further restricted to the set of holomorphic functions, which are bounded and analytic within this domain, forming the space $H^\infty(\Omega)$. We can create an algebraic structure on the set of continuous, linear transformations within this space, denoted as $\mathcal{L}(H^\infty(\Omega))$. Our research focuses on the composition operators within this framework, for which a sufficient condition is provided, involving the boundary behavior of analytic discs within $\Omega$, to ensure that the composed operator $\Phi\circ f$ remains bounded and continuous. Interestingly, in cases where these analytic discs are non-trivial, the composed operator becomes compact. Our research also explores the special case of the polydisc, allowing us to extend our findings to consider the maximal domain of continuity for these composition operators.

We found that anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators in string theory at two loops adhere to specific relations, which follow from the operator product expansion, yielding dimensions in terms of the coupling constant as $\gamma = \frac{2j(j+1)}{g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2} + \frac{2j(j+1)(7j^2+7j-1)}{g_{\mathrm{YM}}^4}$. Additionally, the calculations confirm that certain coefficients in the OPE coefficients vanish for specific operators, which aligns with predictions made through holographic methods. However, the coefficients of the OPE coefficients at two loops do not match the values obtained through holographic calculations.

GPU applications, especially those used in scientific simulations and AI, frequently encounter performance bottlenecks and run-time errors due to inefficient GPU memory usage. Current GPU memory allocators are often incapable of efficiently managing large, dynamic memory needs or are found to have flaws. In response, we developed an memory allocator called DynaSOAr, which utilizes a sophisticated, software-based cache coherency mechanism to manage heterogenous GPU systems with CPU and NVRAM. DynaSOAr integrates this mechanism with an, allocator that is both fast and capable of handling large, dynamic memory requirements. In particular, it utilizes a log-structured approach. Our evaluation of DynaSOAr across numerous GPU-based applications reveals notable gains, with up to 200.00x faster allocation rates, up to a 25.44x improvement in usable GPU memory, and significant storage time reductions. Importantly, no applications exhibited slower storage access times or saw a decrease in overall storage bandwidth.

We examine whether isospin-violating dark matter can escape constraints from direct detection experiments while being produced through kinetic mixing with a hidden photon, part of a Sp(2N) extension of the Peierls-Hamiltonian framework. To do this, we consider two UV completions featuring an abelian gauge group associated with fermion number, specifically SU(2) x U(1)_X and Sp(2N) x U(1)_X. While the inclusion of fermion number symmetry assists in stabilizing dark matter, it also restricts the completion to non-mixing operators, thereby requiring the kinetic mixing to originate through operators that violate U(1)_X. Notably, this enables the evasion of direct detection experiment constraints, even as the dark matter production through kinetic mixing proceeds.

A crucial aspect of building straw tubes is ensuring they are pre-tensioned to an optimal level, which directly impacts their performance in vacuum environments like those found in straw tubes. This study provides a detailed mathematical analysis to determine the minimum pre-tension required, taking into consideration the mechanical properties of straw tubes. Using the principles of material mechanics and finite element methods, we created a comprehensive model that predicts the internal pressure within pre-tensioned tubes. Furthermore, we established a minimum threshold for pre-tension to ensure the straw tube maintains a vacuum without inverting its internal structure. This approach also takes into account the negative Poisson's ratio effect, which describes how the straw tube's cross-sectional dimensions change in response to internal pressure. As a result of this analysis, we developed a practical formula for determining the minimum pre-tension needed, which can be applied across a wide range of straw tube designs.

The capacity to make decisions under uncertain conditions is crucial to the operational abilities of any system or machine. In scenarios where uncertainty arises from unpredictable environmental conditions or dynamic changes, the tolerance of a decision-making system can be measured by the minimum amount of change required in its parameters to render its decisions ineffective. This concept can be generalized to quantify decision function robustness in the presence of uncertain or changing environments. In this research, we have developed robust optimization techniques for training decision function robustness in the context of neural networks. These methods involve optimizing a decision function to maximize its robustness while considering potential shifts in its parameters. Our robust optimization framework can be applied to neural networks with continuous parameters and is based on minimizing the amount of change in its parameters that could render its decisions ineffective. Additionally, we have derived multiple optimization methods and analyzed the relationship between the optimization degree and the robustness of the decision function. Our study also compares the robustness of machine learning models trained using different techniques, such as robustness-optimized neural networks and those regularized with techniques like regularization.

We study the large-amplitude phonon and supersonic phonon (roton) modes in a supersolid composed of a periodic array of oscillating impurities and a superfluid. As a result of the oscillations, the supersonic phonon mode exhibits an increasing frequency, while the phonon mode displays oscillatory behavior. Furthermore, our analysis reveals an energy transfer from the impurity to the superfluid that may induce local heating and affect the system's stability. By investigating the phonon dispersion at large amplitudes, we identify critical thresholds for maintaining supersolid stability. These thresholds depend on various impurity parameters and can be experimentally manipulated.

We conduct a comprehensive analysis of neighbour-transitive codes in generalized quadrangles, confirming earlier findings of Boucher and Leemans. To begin, we define the notion of a neighbour-regular code and demonstrate its self-dual property. Then, we focus on examining neighbour-regular and neighbour-transitive codes within generalized quadrangles, giving particular attention to minimal and maximal examples. An extensive catalog of their types is provided in the process.

We've examined the directional differences in mass distribution within the Central Molecular Zone using the VERA radio interferometer's data on the orbit of the Sgr A* star cluster. Specifically, the second Fourier amplitude coefficient, denoted as $A_2$, indicates a change in elliptical mass distribution that varies with scale. We've also used higher-order harmonics to confirm that lower-order coefficients provide an accurate description of the mass distribution. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the star cluster's orbits are influenced by a central object, the supermassive black hole Sgr A*, and that the mass distribution within roughly 1 pc is not uniformly distributed.

Our study examines the ultra-fast optical properties of metallic nickel using femtosecond pump-probe reflections in a transmission setup. A comprehensive analysis was performed at various wavelengths between 400 nm and 800 nm, and different sample fluences ranging from 0.05 to 2.5 J/cm^2. Fitting experimental data with a two-level model revealed significant changes in the sample's electronic state and energy distribution at higher fluences. These observations suggested a rapid interband transitions and the excitation of hot carriers in the d-band. Furthermore, we investigated how electron redistribution influences non-linear absorption and discovered increased scattering rates as the sample's electronic state approaches its equilibrium at higher fluences.

The infrastructure of any electronic device is heavily reliant on temperature monitoring to guarantee stable and error-free operations. This need has led to the development of a fully digital, temperature-sensing solution grounded in the statistical analysis of intrinsic noise within MOS transistors. The system's effectiveness has been demonstrated to encompass a broad temperature range of -55 to +150°C with exceptional precision and accuracy, surpassing standard temperature specifications by a significant margin. Real-world applications were tested across a wide range of conditions to verify its functionality. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with industry-standard A-class benchmarks was conducted to validate its thermal performance.

We use the quantum scissors technique to create nearly ideal, complex entangled states using only partially entangled resources. A combination of two nonlinear crystals and a beam splitter enables the creation of multipartite entangled polarized photons, which can serve as foundational building blocks for quantum computations. Furthermore, our method yields less noisy multipartite states than previously used methods, offering a more efficient and practical approach to quantum information processing.

This study addresses the cost of IoT device misclassification in a practical and effective manner. By considering the costs of training and testing with labeled data, we develop a method to optimize classification decisions. First, we establish the relationship between misclassification errors and misclassification costs, allowing us to incorporate costs into the classification process. Next, we introduce a technique for learning with misclassified data in a cost-conscious manner. Furthermore, we propose efficient online algorithms for real-time misclassification of IoT devices in stream data and provide a scalability-enhancing approach based on feature extraction. Finally, we validate our approach through numerical experiments with IoT datasets.

We establish a one-to-one correspondence between finite Godel algebras and finite forest structures, demonstrating the specific nature of this relationship. Additionally, we develop a method to represent Godel algebras using a special type of space and a using a special class of functions, thus creating a functional representation. We also define a corresponding relationship using a different set of structures and show its properties, including the preservation of important mathematical operations and properties, a property not seen in Alchourrón, Garcia-Carpintero, and Lupu's work on partial meet revision systems.

Machine-readable corpora that are reasonably sized can still yield aligners capable of surpassing or matching the capabilities of established alignment tools, such as GIZA++. This aligns with broader findings in the field, and we observe the same effect in the context of word alignment. When aligners are evaluated on unseen data, those educated on smaller corpora can outperform or at least compare favorably to those trained on larger corpora. Although it is more challenging for aligners to accurately identify non-existent alignments, those trained on smaller corpora are still able to identify significant majority of present alignments with high levels of accuracy.

The paper introduces an asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm, rooted in Ray-Kravaris' relaxation theory. It focuses on solving monolithic systems with diverse scales, utilizing a multi-grid algorithm with several levels. At each grid level, a Biconjugate Gradient method is employed to iteratively decompose the system, allowing for asynchronous updates of the solution vector by different processors in parallel. The algorithm's effectiveness and non-stationary nature are demonstrated through various 3D fluid flow simulations in porous media.

This research implements the code microlensing.py, a simulation that models the occurrence of black hole events in both PBH and stellar-evolved categories, based on PBH distribution assumptions. Following the successful detection of the first stellar-evolved black hole through the ATLAS collaboration, this study conducts predictions for future ATLAS events, PBH-related microlensing events, and the overall PBH distribution. Furthermore, the code can be adapted for use in other significant surveys, such as the search for dark matter and gravitational waves. Under the assumption of a mean PBH mass of $30\,M_\odot$, there should be approximately 10 times more PBH events than stellar-evolved ones, and PBH events are anticipated to start with an initial magnitude of around $15$.

Due to its one-dimensional nature, systems with dipolar interactions typically exhibit a single ordered phase, characterized by a unique arrangement of dip moments at a packing density below 0.5. However, increasing the packing density beyond 0.5 causes various crystalline phases with alternating and aligned dip moments to emerge as result of various competing interactions among the dipoles. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, it was discovered that two additional frustrated phases with comparable stability emerge. One phase exhibits alternating dip orientations within a honeycomb lattice structure, while the other features aligned dip moments within a kagome lattice. These two phases, in addition to the existing alternating phase, compete at higher packing densities. The competition among these three phases results in two distinct boundaries, defining the phase diagram. Notably, one boundary separates the alternating and honeycomb phases, whereas the other separates the aligned and kagome phases. The behavior at the boundary between the two frustrated phases remains unique, with the system displaying characteristics of both types of ordering.

We investigate the impact of standard differentiation and integration methods on the positive definiteness of zonal functions, and interestingly find that these operations preserve this property when the order is less than or equal to two. However, both differentiation and integration no longer possess a universal application in the analysis of positive definite functions. We instead introduce alternative operators with broader applicability, including a generalized integration method and a novel differential operator that incorporates a parameter, which we observe maintains positive definiteness in all cases. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this new operator establishes a correspondence with a pathway of function transformations analogous to a fractional integration method previously described by Bojani and Vetro.

Our research focuses on interaction-free imaging of low-sensitive samples, which are fragile and easily damaged.  Traditionally, quantum imaging uses the principles of interference and correlation between light and sample to enable interaction-free detection.  However, the negative impact of the imaging process on the sample's state remains unclear.  To address this, our study proposes a quantum imaging technique that can effectively avoid any damage to the sample while achieving interaction-free imaging.  The technique is tested using a simple optical system and sample, which consists of a superposed on/off state and is illuminated by a single-photon source.  By applying two-measurement schemes, we obtain clear images of the sample in the spatial domain.  Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of interaction-free imaging for delicate samples and have the potential for applications in microscopy and astronomy.

This research investigates the emergence of multiple steady flows and how the liquid in foam structures moves. By analyzing flows through interconnected vesicles and comparing the results to a single foam unit, we discover that the liquid's flow behavior changes based on structure. Introducing a 'roughness factor' that quantifies this discrepancy, we find it increases with more complex foam formations. Our findings align with experiments, offering new insights into the dynamics of liquid inside foam structures. Additionally, we validate our results, contributing to understanding the flow dynamics within foam for applications like carbon sequestration and oil extraction.

Deep convolutional neural networks have demonstrated exceptional capability in handling a variety of vision tasks. Nonetheless, their performance can be hindered by inherent uncertainty. By employing an ensemble method, multiple distinct CNN architectures are trained on the same dataset, thereby mitigating this uncertainty and boosting overall performance. In our research, we leverage an ensemble of convolutional neural networks to further enhance performance for the 19-CAT dataset, a collection of images categorized into 20 distinct classes.

Researchers employed electron energy loss spectroscopy to examine dipolar electron-hole excitations in sodium particles with a 25-nanometer diameter. By comparing these findings to monopole hole excitations, the mass enhancement for the dipolar excitations was determined to be roughly 3.5 times, significantly higher than the 2.4 times mass enhancement observed in monopole hole excitations.

We provide an in-depth analysis of work at the level of individual microstates, building upon recent advancements in statistical mechanics. We identify a limitation in the standard definition of work that has led to varied interpretations, particularly in distinguishing between dissipated work and excess work. By re-evaluating the definition, we find that the work done on a microstate can be broken down into two components: energy stored in that microstate and heat dissipated as a deviation from equilibrium. This component is always non-negative and reflects the magnitude of fluctuations in the system. We apply our revised definition to investigate the components of work in small systems, and demonstrate its relevance to studies on nonequilibrium thermodynamic relations and irreversibility.

Cotangent bundle cases in quantum field theory demonstrate significant simplifications. Exploring the quantum corrections of FLP formulas, we found that FLP formulas can be applied to any symplectic manifold through the use of FLP deformation. An adaptation of FLP formulas for cotangent bundle cases, developed by splitting the FLP deformation, yields streamlined expressions. This approach is illustrated with an explicit example, namely the free spin path integral.

We continue our examination of the modulated stability in gap solitons from a previously published analysis and expand upon the findings. Our study now includes two more exponentially weak effects, which significantly impact the stability profile, particularly at the base frequency where the gap solitons are situated. To accurately represent the minimal points of the dispersion relation, we developed an improved theoretical model that accurately captures the behavior of hertzian springs, unlike our earlier model valid at extremely low base frequencies. This theoretical model allows us to investigate the minimal points of the dispersion relation when gap solitons are positioned at arbitrary locations. To illustrate the size-dependent behavior in large-amplitude gap solitons, we conducted numerical simulations that reveal two distinct regions with different stability patterns, which can be attributed to the interaction between two non-linear wave phenomena. These gap solitons exhibit stability at lower base frequencies but become unstable at higher frequencies, whereas, for larger sizes, they display reversed stability patterns, with exponential instability at lower base frequencies, followed by stability, and then pattern repetition, resulting in the formation of localized wave structures.

We investigate a specific type of feature in inflation models that can be linked to a symmetry in the scalar sector of the inflaton field. Our analysis focuses on how this symmetry affects the scale-dependent signatures of primordial non-Gaussianity within a single-field inflation model. By applying an $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry to the potential, the peaks in non-Gaussian correlations are shifted by approximately one order of magnitude, whereas applying a continuous $U(1)$ symmetry introduces an additional factor of inflaton field normalization that significantly amplizes their effect, potentially by three orders of magnitude. We also explore how features in single-field inflation non-Gaussianities can be distinguished from those in multi-field inflation models, noting that multi-field features are usually confined to a specific helium density component rather than being universally present.

The accordion graph class $A[n,k]$ is an inherently built graph with $fk$ vertices and naturally constructs as a subgraph of the hexagonal grid. Here, $f=\frac{3nk-2(n+k)}{2}$ and $k$ is at least 2. We demonstrate that a graph in the accordion class $A[n,k]$ is non-circulant when $k$ is at least 2, and it is isomorphic to the Petersen graph when it has 10 vertices. We also establish a circumvention center set of the accordion class $A[n,k]$ with size 1, and determine the order of the circumvention radius and diameter of the accordion class $A[n,k]$.

In this study, we examine the temporal evolution of the participation ratio in a one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walk featuring varying coin parameters. These parameters remain constant within specific intervals but change at irregular intervals, mimicking a quantum walk with disordered coins. To investigate the transition from localized to delocalized states, we performed a numerical analysis of the critical critical phenomenon, resulting in accurate critical exponents for both the participation ratio and the participation exponent in the near-critical regime. Additionally, we demonstrate that the participation ratio exhibits self-similar behavior and follows a universal scaling law, which we also explore in the context of finite-size effects.

Recent findings from the ImageNet leaderboard show that pre-trained foundation models, like ViT, can be significantly outperformed by pre-trained ImageNet top models. This suggests that supervised fine-tuning of pre-trained ViT on ImageNet is an overlooked method for pre-training vision transformers. In this study, we re-examined fine-tuning ViT on ImageNet and proposed novel strategies to pre-train ViT. Our pre-training methods involve using different augmentations, supervising ViT's output with ViT+CNN ensemble, and combining this with DINO self-supervision. With these techniques, our method improved the existing self-supervised method by 0.4% in top-1 accuracy. Additionally, with these strategies, our method increased the gap between self-supervised and supervised pre-training by 6.8% with state-of-the-art augmentations. Our code is available on GitHub.

Within the framework of $f(T)$ modified gravity, where the gravitational Lagrangian is linear in the $T$ modification of the Weyl scalar, a perfect fluid model is analyzed. This fluid, with its viscosity dependent on the universe's evolutionary rate, is shown to satisfy requirements for the absence of ghost and breach problems, as well as the fulfillment of the dominant, strong, and non-negative energy conditions. When the model is perturbed, it exhibits a relationship between the speed of perturbations and the background Weyl tensor, leading to the conclusion that speed is non-zero. Furthermore, by drawing analogies with $\Lambda$CDM, $\Lambda$RT, and specific forms of Bardeen-Radner models, a fluid is described that meets all necessary requirements for validity. By restricting the model parameters, a universe phase consisting of radiation, a quantum-dominated universe, and a universe dominated by viscosity, along with an accelerating universe phase, is found to occur sequentially. Additionally, considering a fluid analogous to dark energy, a model similar to $\Lambda$CDM, with an equation of state resembling that of dark energy, is described. This model also exhibits statephases similar to those of dark energy in general relativity when certain model parameters are chosen.

The Cauchy problem for incompressible Euler equations exhibits well-posedness in dimensions up to four, but we demonstrate that it is neither well- nor uniquely posed in dimensions five or more, based on a construction by Tsai. Furthermore, using a different method, we show that the incompressible Euler equations are not well-posed within the space of bounded vector fields.

Artificial intelligence tools, particularly large language models and visual generative models, offer users considerable assistance and control in various processes. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms of these systems remain shrouded in mystery for average users, limiting their ability to fully utilize and direct AI capabilities. Existing solutions primarily designed for developers and experts in the field fall short in empowering everyday users to make significant changes to their workflows.

This research introduces "Stable Artist," an interactive system that collaborates with users to maximize AI-assisted benefits. By engaging users in the image generation process through a series of structured interactions, Stable Artist amplifies their control and provides insights into the effects of each decision. Furthermore, by gathering user feedback and continuously refining its model, Stable Artist accumulates personal knowledge tailored to each user's preferences.

Our results reveal that Stable Artist enables users to create high-quality images more efficiently, consistently, and effectively, by leveraging AI as a thoughtful partner that adapts to their evolving needs and desires.

Deep learning's array of black-box models, renowned for their flexibility, often yield inaccurate or uncertain predictions when confronted with unseen data. To address this shortcoming, a low-cost Bayesian method is presented for assessing the reliability of predictive models' outputs, specifically their end-to-end probability distributions. To mitigate the limitations of traditional likelihood-free inference methods' computational demands, a simplified approach is adopted, utilizing neural density estimators, a flexible class of approximations, within a framework that relies on pre-trained models, without the need for customised training. This method's feasibility is demonstrated through its application to existing, pre-trained models, using public datasets, and it's shown to provide a reliable estimate of prediction uncertainty, in contrast to point-wise estimates. Furthermore, experiments using synthetic data reveal that our method outperforms competing alternatives in accurately capturing the distribution of latent variables.

The LHC can establish constraints on a single nucleon cross—section, which is used to describe low-mass dark matter (DM) nucleon scattering, by utilizing the $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ decay and $p p \to j + \text{mono-jet}$ process at 13 TeV. These constraints are derived from an analysis of events with one jet and significant missing transverse momentum using LHC data that was collected in 2016. After applying analysis techniques, the resultant constraints are then compared with those from the LHC's primary search for DM. The discovery is contingent upon a 35.8 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity.

We present initial results from the study of the horizontal component of the solar magnetic field using the HIRES simulator, a virtual reality tool, in conjunction with the DRMS database. The HIRES simulator takes the magnetic field data and converts it into a three-dimensional magnetic field visualization that can be experienced in a three-dimensional environment. The HIRES simulator also incorporates the movement of magnetic bright points and other solar features to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the solar surface. The HIRES simulator has been successfully integrated with the DRMS database and the magnetic field visualization has been improved and the user interface has been user-friendly.

The rise of video technology on social media platforms has led to an explosion in the amount of video content being shared online. This has significantly changed the landscape of data availability for vision and language-based AI applications, specifically in the area of dynamic human activities. To address the scarcity of informative data sources in this field, we propose the use of minimal videos - extremely short and often single-frame animations - as a medium to understand the dynamics of human behavior. Our study focuses on leveraging the knowledge contained within minimal videos to enhance our understanding of dynamic vision, as these videos reflect a broader spectrum of human activities due to their diverse creation processes. We present three datasets consisting of transition sequences for action recognition, skeleton extraction, and pose estimation, thereby demonstrating the potential to pre-train models using minimal videos and achieve improved performance on related, short video tasks.

We utilize the 't Hooft-Mandelstam dual superconductivity model in which a monopole's magnetic flux tube interacts with an external magnetic field. Through exact solutions for the coupled Seiberg-Witten and Abelian Higgs equations, we find that bound monopole ground states achieve stability and localize when the magnetic field is sufficiently high. Conversely, they decompose as the magnetic field is weakened below a critical threshold. The localized states exhibit an approximate Gaussian pattern, with the underlying flux tube length determined by a balance between the external magnetic energy and the non-Abelian flux tube's intrinsic tension.

Deep learning based weather forecasting models have gained popularity in recent years, with several recent studies evaluating their performance in various contexts. Since data-driven methods are commonly used in forecasting, it's essential to examine how different data representations and preprocessing approaches influence both the forecasts and evaluation results. We investigated the effects of three data normalization strategies, using the MediFor dataset in two sets of forecasting experiments, which we analyzed in two ways: in original form and as suggested by the benchmark in advanced neural network-based short-term weather forecasting.

In models involving multiple dark matter candidates, such as the three-Higgs-doublet model with a dark sector, finding completely symmetric potential models is challenging. The inclusion of CP-violation expands the model's parameter space, enabling darker matter interaction and expanding its mass range from a few hundred GeV to a few TeV. The complexity of finding symmetric models with more than two dark matter candidates increases due to the required interference between multiple annihilation channels. The region where all annihilation channels interfere constructively becomes significantly larger with multiple dark matter candidates, and for six fermionic DM candidates, it can increase by over 100 times. Furthermore, such models with multiple dark matter candidates are favored by future experiments at the ILC and FCC-eh.

Recent research has broadened the PPT square conjecture's scope to encompass various mathematical setups, such as real/complex numbers, finite fields, quaternions, and specific matrix structures. Our study extends this exploration to dimension P matrices, demonstrating that the PPT square conjecture holds true in these scenarios. Additionally, we address the PPT cube conjecture, proving its validity for certain cases and providing a detailed analysis for the rest.

The efficient delivery of cargo to remote neural locations relies on the formation of tree-like structures through branching. To gain a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing this process, we developed a new model that describes how self-associating proteins, such as MAP2, influence transport dynamics within straight and curved microtubules. Our results demonstrate that variations in the bending radius and the presence of protein clusters can either accelerate or decrease the jump length of moving cargo. Specifically, certain conditions like high protein cluster sizes or intermediate curvature radii have the potential to enhance transport. Our study provides valuable insights into the underlying factors that contribute to the development of complex, branching tree structures in neural systems.

In the realm of graph-based learning, creating synthetic data is essential for developing algorithms and evaluating their performance. Graph generation, in particular, remains a complex challenge. Existing methods fall short for real-world applications such as banking transaction networks due to their inability to generate intricate and complex graphs that mirror banking transactions. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel approach for generating banking graphs using the SMOTE technique and a new data analysis method. Our method ensures the creation of realistic and valid banking networks by generating accurate table data while maintaining node and edge validity. We incorporate a new fraud detection algorithm that leverages the synthesized data to detect anomalies in banking transactions.

In the process of a white dwarf star being torn apart by a black hole's gravitational forces, ejected material may form an acccretion disc around the black hole, potentially leading to observable flares through the emission of synchrotron radiation, particularly at millimeter wavelengths. A theoretical model has been developed to estimate the time-dependent size and mass of this accretion disc. According to this model, the disc initially expands rapidly at the rate of several thousand kilometers per second before gradually slowing down and reaching equilibrium after a period of tens of minutes to hours. The model also considers the thickness and outer boundary of the disc, as well as the molecular composition, particularly water and carbon monoxide, present in the disc. These molecules are predicted to emit significant signals at millimeter frequencies, which could be detected by state-of-the-art telescopes such as the Next Generation Very Large Array and the millimeter subarray of the Interferometer for Gravitational wave Astronomy, even hours to days after the supernova event.

The study of crossovers in CP violations within semileptonic tau decays is an
important area of research, and it is only beginning to be explored due to the
increized interest in this topic. With the technological advancements, the
possibility of exploring CP violations in three-body semileptonic tau decays
has become more realistic, particularly with the potential improvements in the
LEP data and the data that could be collected at an ILC or a FCC-ee. To further
investigate CP violations, the analysis should prioritize three-body tau decays
as they offer more opportunities for violations of CP and are less affected by
systematic errors. The potential source of CP violations in these decays could
be attributed to the mixing between the neutral B mesons, and the analysis in this
study will provide the necessary theoretical framework, the required parameters,
and specific three-body semileptonic tau decays that could be studied.

This study employs differential topology to examine the metric space defined by Tversky ratio models, used to understand human cognitive maps of concept associations. Specifically, it investigates two key model components, similarity and interestingness, across parametrized spaces of specific sizes. By analyzing these metrics, the research identifies their boundary points, extreme forms, and continuous subspaces corresponding to unique topological characteristics, while also visualizing their topological structures.

This work presents a deconvolution-based deblurring structure, featuring a unique reblurring component to counteract excessive deblurring and underdeblurring outcomes prevalent in existing methods. The resampling technique used in the reblurring module mimics physical phenomena to improve edge reconstruction. To enhance its performance, the reblurring module is integrated prior to the non-local mean post-processing, as experimental results confirm that initial reblurring enhances the non-local mean module's non-local pattern estimation. Moreover, the reblurring module's incorporation accelerates the non-local mean module, as fewer iterations are required to achieve satisfactory results due to improved edge reconstruction in the initial stages. Consequently, this leads to enhanced deblurring performance.

Recent discoveries in neuroscience and machine learning (CRNs and neural nets, respectively) seem to share parallels.  The autonomous learning observed in both fields can be explained by the dynamics underlying these systems.  This work reveals a fundamental link between these dynamics and the autonomous learning behavior they exhibit, drawing on the Wigner-Jordan algebraic representation of Schrodinger's equation to establish a mathematical equivalence between CRNs and neural nets.  By highlighting this connection, we open up opportunities for cross-fertilization of ideas and insights across these fields, ultimately enriching both artificial and biological learning research.  To validate our findings, we replicate the learning characteristics of a previously proposed neural model using the corresponding autonomous CRN.  The successful mapping of neural models to CRNs provides a versatile framework for exploring and developing new artificial neural models, while potentially offering valuable insights into neuronal processing, as illustrated by our demonstration.

We investigate the concept of open completeness in countable forcing notions, with a particular emphasis on its relation to ultrafilters. The concept of open completeness is introduced, and a thorough exploration is provided, including its connection to other fortementsian properties. The concept is shown to be inherently countable, and an example of a non-open-complete ccc forcing is presented. The property of open completeness is demonstrated to be closed under countable products and a specific type of embedding. The ultrapower of an original forcing according to a countable saturated ultrafilter is shown to be open-complete if the original forcing has a sufficient density of points. Additionally, it is found that the ccc property is closed under countable ultrapower extensions using countably saturated ultrafilters.

To evaluate the efficiency of scientific computing systems, data-driven science approaches analyze the scientific code in question. However, such methodology faces a challenge: the scientific code is seldom easy to run or access. Therefore, we suggest an alternative, fully automatic benchmarking process that operates online, fully leveraging the scientific code itself. Our approach involves two key components - first, executing a light-weight model multiple times under controlled conditions to obtain accurate benchmarks. Secondly, optimizing the statistical analysis of these benchmarks through multiple criteria. These strategies notably improve the reliability and accuracy of benchmarking through current infrastructure.

We provide proof for two related concepts: (1) it can be shown that if a graph does not contain a specific smaller graph as a significant part, it has a limited number of colors needed; (2) this  limit can be represented by structures with particular properties when the limited number is just three.

This paper investigates an adaptive cost function, and a simulation-based study is conducted to determine the effect of function convexity and the regulation parameter on its efficiency. The results indicate that an optimally selected regulation parameter is crucial, and its success heavily depends on cost function convexity. Furthermore, a more symmetric and thus more convex signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) cost function is shown to be optimally optimized more rapidly.

To effectively utilize quantum correlations in measurement, a necessary condition is the precise generation of specific atomic states. In this study, an original approach is proposed for creating highly entangled atomic pairs through the entangling of remotely located atoms using their shared environment, based on a scheme developed by Polzik et al. [Nature 430, 283 (2004)]. Our proposed method involves inducing entangling collisions at different stages, resulting in a range of multi-partite states with varying degrees of utility in quantum metrology. We demonstrate that the final state's sensitivity can be significantly enhanced through the application of a single, joint measurement and subsequent post-processing of results. Additionally, a theoretical framework is derived, enabling the analysis of large systems composed of N/2 spatially separated pairs of atoms (A and B) undergoing M controlled-Z interactions. Our approach is applicable not only to optical systems but also to systems based on cold atoms or photons, where it results in the creation of GHZ states.

This study explores the behavior of the lowest Robin eigenvalue in the anisotropic p-Laplace problem, given the constraint of a fixed p-Laplacian volume. Utilizing a combination of a loose upper bound derived from the isoperimetric inequality and the sharp lower bound of the sharp anisotropic Sobolev inequality, we determine that this lowest Robin eigenvalue either monotonically decreases or increases based on the parameter $ \beta $ in the boundary integral, for a fixed isoperimetric constant.

Recently, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been successfully applied to
graph learning problems, but the generalization of GCNs to other data types
hasn't been explored extensively. In this paper, a novel perspective is presented,
demonstrating that popular CNN and FC network architectures can be viewed as GCNs
with specific graph structures and generalization capabilities. Furthermore, an
explicit connection between CNN/FC networks and GCNs is established. Based on
this generalization, a graph learning framework is proposed, allowing GCNs to
process data from images, texts, and other domains in addition to graphs.

This paper presents an enhanced stochastic parsing algorithm named Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), which builds on top of the VIGOR parser. DCST leverages self-training, a technique that uses a model's predictions on unlabelled data to reinforce its training. Unlike prior self-training methods, DCST self-training is performed within a framework that accounts for the uncertainty in model predictions. This is achieved through the integration of two key components: Deep Contextualization, which contextualizes words based on their surrounding terms and vice versa, and Selective Self-training, a mechanism that identifies the most informative unlabelled sentences to a model. These innovations enable DCST to surpass the previously best self-training approach, significantly enhancing the model's accuracy and convergence rate. Our experiments, which utilize the Conll shared task datasets, demonstrate the efficacy of DCST in parsing tasks.

We present updated measurements of the branching fractions for the decays B^- -> D^(*)0 tau^- anti-nu_tau and compare them to the corresponding muonic andronic decays. The ratio of the tauonic to the muonic or lamonic branching fraction is found to be 0.87±0.05 (stat.) ± 0.05 (syst.) ± 0.02 (EW) for D and 0.92±0.06 (stat.) ± 0.05 (syst.) ± 0.02 (EW) for D_, with an assumed f_(b/s) of 0.494 ± 0.005 ± 0.013. The precision of this measurement is limited by the knowledge of radiative corrections. The results are also compared to the predictions of the standard model, which are in good agreement with the measured values.

A comprehensive approach to identifying and calculating properties of non-invertible symmetries is presented, encompassing unitary global symmetries, higher-form symmetries, and non-invertible operators within a unified framework. By representing these concepts as nodes in a diagrammatic network, their generation, fusions, and constraints can be analyzed and calculated systematically. This approach enables a rigorous derivation of fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries, supplemented by a set of higher-level consistency requirements. As a practical application, we recover key aspects of lattice models, including Ising and quantum double, and in three dimensions, we derive fusion rules for discrete T-duality symmetries in terms of gapped data, while exploring the implications for an exemplar field theory through an extension of our methodology.

We are examining an extension of CPT logic by adding an ability to assert the existence or nonexistence of solutions to systems of linear equations over a finite field. C, the base temporal logic, includes a set of finite-state processes and traces as its models. The problem of determining if a set of linear equations has a satisfying assignment is generally a difficult one, but becomes more manageable when the coefficients and the field in question are both small and finite. C already has a means of defining relations involving powers of generators in a field to its models. Building on this foundation, we're exploring whether we can also define the connection between these powers and the field's additive structure within CPT. Specifically, we're looking at unordered linear equations of the form $\sum a_i \cdot \gamma^{i} = b$, where the coefficients and $b$ are elements of the field, in relation to the $\equiv$ relation.

This study presents neutron and x-ray resonant inelastic x-ray scattering measurements on the series (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir_2O_7 for x = 0, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4.  These materials exhibit a series of changes in their magnetic properties and electronic structure as the Bi content increases.  Neutron data on the materials for x = 0, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25 show that they exhibit a series of changes in their magnetic properties and electronic structure.  These were determined by analyzing valence band spectra and higher energy spectra.  Analysis of these spectra reveals that the valence band is composed of Bi 6s and Eu 5d and f states for x ≤ 0.25.  These features disappear, however, for x ≥ 0.3, indicating a significant change in the materials electronic structure.  Analysis of core-level spectra also shows Bi-related features at the Bi edge.  These were quantified and revealed increases in Bi-related features as the Bi content increased.  This indicates that the materials surface is contaminated with Bi for x ≤ 0.2.  These results have implications for understanding the materials magnetic properties and electronic structure.

Consider a set-valued mapping defined on a Banach space, whose values are convex closed subsets of another Banach space, all contained within a bounded and closed region of the first Banach space. A Lipschitz selection for this set-valued mapping is guaranteed to exist if its graph has a certain level of 'thickness', measured by a concept known as the radius, in a metric space defined by the two Banach spaces. This result represents a sharp extension of existing results, including those obtained when considering set-valued mappings with compact convex values or when the set-valued mapping is considered to be a projection, all under conditions related to the diameter or diameter of the set-valued mapping.

To illustrate the concept of nontransitivity in n-tuples, consider n dice labeled 1 through n, where each die has faces numbered 1 through 6. When these dice are thrown simultaneously, the probability that a higher-numbered die shows a greater number than a lower-numbered die is not necessarily 2/3. The purpose of this paper is to provide a systematic method for identifying nontransitive n-tuples by presenting a systematic algorithm to systematically enumerate all such tuples.

System administrators have the ability to control system run-time settings through kernel parameters.  It is also possible for users to modify run-time settings themselves, allowing a single system to operate in multiple configurations.  However, unnecessary run-time options can lead to unanticipated system behavior and increased system performance costs, according to a recently discovered paper.  This system could either remove unused run-time options, requiring a system reboot, or provide an interface to dynamically remove options without the need for reboots.  Both methods were tested with a system that supports the Linux OS.

To effectively identify nuclei ionisation as a signature for detecting nuclear recoil events, a novel simulation for dark matter-nuclei scattering with varied nuclear sizes and compositions is developed. This is achieved using existing neutron capture simulations, and their ionisation yields for individual neutrons and protons are combined in accordance with specific nuclei configurations. By incorporating this into existing dark matter-nuclei simulation frameworks, such as GEANT, this approach enables the direct comparison of nucleii ionisation and recoil events, ultimately aiding in the understanding of the non-linear relationship between these phenomena.

Quantum information is being exchanged between coherent quantum systems, where the flow of this information is being tracked and manipulated.  The process of quantum-state-exchange (QSE) is being explored in systems consisting of two-way coupled qubits.  However, due to technical limitations in measuring this information exchange efficiently, only one-directional QSE was demonstrated in previous studies.  Two-way QSE has since been conceptualized and was experimentally realized using superconducting qubits and polaritonic qubits.  Specifically, the researchers studied the dynamics of an entangled anti-polariton state, where two photons are shared between two qubits in a bosonic resonator.  Due to the rapid loss of photons, this experiment utilized the rapid QSE between the anti-polariton and qubit states.  The progress of this information exchange was quantified by measuring the fidelity of teleported states, and was found to exceed the theoretical limits of analogous systems based on fermionic particles.  Specifically, the experiment showed that the fidelity of quantum-state-teleportation using the entangled anti-polariton qubit state exceeds that of using entangled quasi-spin-1/2 states.  This achievement was made possible by the rapid QSE between the anti-polariton and qubit degrees-of-freedom, and was found to occur at a rate that exceeds the inherent decay rate of the resonator by a factor of 1000.

Deep learning techniques can effectively extract inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from noisy ECG signals, however, these techniques often struggle with rR peak detection on entire signal databases, and many existing EGI extraction frameworks rely on pre-computed or manually rR-peaked ECG data, which may not be representative of real-world conditions. To address these issues, this study proposes a end-to-end ECI extraction framework that can accurately process entire ECG databases, including detecting rR peaks, extracting IBIs, and classifying arrhythmias, and can be compared with existing state-of-the-art methods. The proposed framework was developed by modifying a existing model known as S-MLP, and by adding modules to extract and classify features from entire ECG databases. The proposed model demonstrated a remarkable accuracy of 98.9% on the PTB-BLUTE dataset, which is significantly higher than that of state-of-the-art methods.

This study explores the role of active systems subject to external potentials, utilizing the active fluctuation dissipation theorem to analyze external potential effects on active particles. Unlike passive systems in harmonic and anharmonic potentials, this work demonstrates that in the presence of active forces, fluctuations exhibit universal behavior irrespective of the potential type. Furthermore, this study reveals that fluctuations can be categorized based on the active force multipole orders of $n=1,2,3$. Specifically, in the presence of active forces with multipole orders of $n=1$ and $n=3$, fluctuations maintain both translational and rotational universal behavior, whereas in the presence of active forces with multipole order of $n=2$, fluctuations exhibit universal behavior only, excluding universal pressure fluctuation. Numerical simulations for active particles in harmonic and anharmonic potentials validate the theoretical predictions of this work.

To develop realistic 3D models of human emotions, it is essential to have accurate meshes that capture the subtle movements of facial features. However, the process of manually creating these meshes is both time-consuming and labor-intensive, while automated systems often struggle to reproduce precise vertex displacements for specific emotions. To address these challenges, we present a novel approach, Unified Human Bone-based Mesh Deformation Imitation, which leverages the inherent relationships between various facial expressions and maps them to corresponding bone deformations, thereby enabling the reproduction of realistic emotions through bone transformations. By incorporating a realistic system bone template, the proposed method facilitates the generalization of this approach to different individuals and models, while ensuring that the predicted outcomes remain consistent and reliable. Experimental evaluations on various datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of HUMBI in achieving accurate emotion replication and its generalizability to new subjects and 3D models.

We present a unified framework for training a single language-agnostic model across multiple languages, powered by a weakly-supervised multilingual framework that leverages unlabelled web data to enhance model performance without the need for additional manual annotation efforts. Our approach initially involves training a separate word-embedding model for each language using a specific objective function. Next, we use these embeddings to sample unlabelled web sentences and apply weak supervision to create relaxed training objectives sentence by sentence. Sampled sentences and originally used training data are combined to create a rich diverse dataset, which is used to train a single multilingual model under a relaxed objective function. Finally, we refine the model using self-training iterations to improve its performance. Our multilingual framework successfully achieves high model accuracy across all individual monolingual tasks and delivers state-of-the-art results on several multilingual NLP tasks.

BasicVSR++ is an enhanced version of BasicVSR, a widely-used video super-resolution model. It.
 leverages the power of rich feature interactions to improve image quality, but its high
 computation demands hinder its practical use in real-world applications. We introduce
 a new approach, non-local feature distillation, to boost the richness of final network
 features, surpassing real-world video super-resolution models. As a result, BasicVSR++
 outperforms the original by a notable margin, achieving a 0.22 in PSNR and 2.4F/
 10F in CHF. This improvement comes at the cost of reduced computational efficiency,
 making BasicVSR++ a superior and practical method for video super-resolution.

Reinforcement learning via trial and error in complex scenarios can be expedited by leveraging prior knowledge, particularly when a series of related tasks must be accomplished. To this end, we introduce a novel approach to multi-task reinforcement learning where several similar but distinct dynamics problems are unified beneath a single, dynamically learned model. While this method facilitates quick adaptation to individual tasks, it may result in compromised performance due to an altered version of each task's true dynamics. To mitigate this issue, we suggest providing the learning algorithm with a pre-established representation of the tasks' structure in order to accelerate adaptation while preserving accuracy. Our method is demonstrated to be particularly efficient when applications involve robotic control and adaptive development.

A theoretical model, known as the two-stroke heat-stroke heat engine, utilizes heat baths of finite size to reheat particles between strokes. The heat absorbed during each stroke drives the engine's power output, which is analyzed in relation to the scaling parameter and the duration of each stroke. The results indicate that the parameter significantly influences both optimal power output and efficiency, whereas a longer stroke duration tends to enhance efficiency while having a more complex effect on the optimal thermal conductivity. The duration also plays a crucial role in the existence of a maximum efficiency, which is explored in detail.

Assessing the impact of hurricanes on power grids through probabilistic modeling is crucial for understanding potential losses and strengthening grid resilience. Evaluating hurricane risk requires in-depth knowledge of power grid geography and historical hurricane tracks and intensities. This study utilizes Dataset6 from the Electricity Loss Due to Disasters database to analyze the loss of generation capacity and load capacity caused by past hurricanes in Florida. By applying a novel method that incorporates nearest weather station data and spatial interpolation, this research calculates the intensity of 237 historical hurricanes in Florida for the period of 1969-2018. Combining this data with high-resolution power system geography from Reliability Assessment of Electric Networks software, this study evaluates the loss of generation capacity and power load caused by each hurricane. The generated dataset, providing insight into the loss of power capacity caused by historical hurricanes, can be employed to develop statistical models that estimate the probability distribution of potential hurricane impacts on the Florida power grid.
We derive a Hadamard's three circles theorem for monogenic functions with respect to the $L^p$-norm across $\mathbb{R}^p$, as well as establish a corresponding result for $p$-monogenic functions.

We've analyzed a unique dynamic system consisting of a countably infinite number of affine mappings on the real number line, which falls within the domain of inverse branches for a specific type of expanding map. This system is fully integrable, with its natural coding space linked to the Dyck System, a formal language. Furthermore, the measure-theoretic and cohomological properties of this system are investigated, revealing that it is both simple and characterized by the reduced Gelfand dual of the Salié series.

The growing list of particle physics models featuring additional scalar particles underscores the necessity for thorough research on their production and interactions at high-luminosity colliders such as the Future Circular Collider and the Large-Ip Large-Ring Colliders. This is particularly true for "vanilla" models, which include the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model, its extensions, the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, and the Standard Model with extra particles, all of which can be rigorously tested with increased luminosity. By supplementing the existing strategies of the LHC, future colliders will offer a wide range of overlapping search techniques, focusing on the most sensitive tests in the mass region between a few TeV and a few hundred GeV. The improved sensitivity will allow for a wide variety of model tests and will open new avenues for discovering new particle physics beyond the Standard Model.

Cascaded arithmetic operations on random variables can effectively model complex, periodic signals, and this concept extends to quasi-periodic signals, and particularly to speech. Employing a multi-layered network design, this research proposes a new system that facilitates the efficient computation of non-linear signals via a sequence of simplified operations. Leveraging this system, a speech model has been developed, and compared to existing random arithmetic models, it demonstrates enhanced capacity for modeling speech with distinct spectral characteristics, including formant structure. Furthermore, this model exhibits robust generalization, accurately reconstructing test speech data without fine-tuning. By translating random variables into numerical values, this model also yields potential applications in the synthesis of realistic speech sounds.

This paper introduces a novel USBFC approach, which utilizes biclustering for collaborative filtering. A significant drawback of current biclustering-based Collaborative Filtering (CF) techniques is their inability to provide a clear explanation of the CF recommendations they generate. To address this issue, USBTC, a USBFC technique, was recently developed, enhancing the accuracy of conventional CF methods by focusing on their scalability. However, USBTC's lack of transparency hinders users from understanding the recommendations it produces. USBTC's process can be summarized as follows: it divides users into distinct groups based on their similarities, analyzes each group's underlying pattern, and calculates the average pattern among the other groups to calculate the user's rating predictions. In this research, we improve USBTC in two key aspects: (1) we modify the cluster formation process to represent each group of users' preferences in a more coherent and understandable pattern, and (2) we incorporate explicit explanations for the CF recommendations we generate, based on the patterns we've identified. Experimental evaluations using three real-world datasets have shown the proposed method to outperform its predecessors, including Vondra's, USBTC, and USBTC with AP, while also providing more comprehensible and transparent recommendations.

For years, researchers have been exploring the possibility of detecting magnetic activity on nearby stars using the JWST. Although earlier studies found that mid-infrared photometry, such as MIRLUS and MIRIAGE surveys, failed to reveal clear indicators of activity like increased H-alpha activity, faster JWST spectroscopy may yield positive results due to its reduced noise levels. In a more recent investigation, the mid-infrared features of three active stars were analyzed using high-resolution JWST observations, which showed that these signals are significantly distorted by molecular bands, making it difficult to detect heightened activity. Consequently, active stars may not stand out against quieter stars in the mid-infrared domain.

To measure topological properties and distinguish between Majorana and non-Majorana effects in hybrid nanowires, it is necessary to analyze thermal behavior at low temperatures. A two-terminal transport measurement was used to characterize thermal characteristics of nanowires made of indium arsenide and aluminum. The investigation revealed the presence of a zero-energy feature caused by multiple phenomena, including thermal broadening, finite temperature effects, and interference between thermal conductance contributions from opposite directions. These non-Majorana processes can show similar patterns to the signature of a topological energy gap. The analysis also takes into account the impact of non-Majorana on a zero-energy peak through a detailed examination of the relevant physical mechanisms and their mathematical representations.

Building on the work of Ausoni and K\'emi\'e, this article develops a bicategorical framework for topological Hochschild homology and shifts to a bicategory level, where the topological homology is now represented as a shadow. It examines the topological Barratt–Priddy–Miller spectrum, denoted as $\bm{BP}$, and calculates its topological homology and the corresponding shadow of $\bm{BP}$. As an application, the topological homology of the topological $K(n)$-local sphere, $LP_{K(n)}\mathbb{S}$, is computed by using a localized version of the BP-van Mill spectrum, $LP_{K(n)}\bm{BP}$.

Images are composed of various elements including color, texture, and arrangement, some of which are crucial to their overall appearance, while others are not as important. To capture images more efficiently, we want to exclude unnecessary information like rotation or background. A novel encoding technique is proposed that learns to separate and style images based on artistic principles, and can be combined with a content encoder. This content encoder focuses only on the meaningful aspects of the image, like a portrait. Our style learning method outperforms existing techniques like PCA or VAE in capturing the underlying styles of a dataset, and is more robust to visual distractions. Our style encoder also outshines previous approaches in separating styled and unstyled images, and is more versatile in capturing multiple styles simultaneously.

In video understanding tasks, there is a pressing need to create a unified representation for both spatial and temporal data, with existing solutions often individually addressing spatial and temporal aspects. We address this gap by integrating spatial and temporal unification within our proposed framework, Feature Mapping Attitude. We propose a context-based ground module attention mechanism that selectively filters out noise from videos, and our experiments on action recognition and temporal action detection demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, particularly when applied to widely-used video understanding models. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhenghangz/FMA.

This research investigates how various physical factors influence the settling velocity and associated dynamics of snow particles in different turbulence intensity levels. By analyzing data from laboratory-extracted synthetic snow particles, we evaluated how these materials respond to different Reynolds numbers, focusing on the effect of Stokes numbers ranging from 0.01 to 0.5. This range corresponds to a non-dimensional viscosity of 0.03, suggesting that snow particles often exhibit intermediate behavior. Our analysis involved examining the angular velocity, rotation periods, and list-wise and measured settling velocities of individual particles. By comparing these findings to previously developed models, we found that existing correlations provide a reasonable estimate of snow particle settling speeds, with values between -0.2 and -0.8, indicating that models may overestimate or underestimate settling velocities depending on the specific turbulence conditions. Furthermore, we discovered that snow particles experience increased rotation rates in more turbulent flows, with values ranging from 1.2 to 1.8, suggesting that models may underestimate rotation rates by up to a factor of two in certain situations.

Deep learning models have gained significant attention in areas like real-world sensory data analysis and synthesis as well as latent space learning and generation. Recent research has integrated generative models with other deep learning architectures, leading to impressive results. This paper provides a thorough examination of the latest advances in deep generative models in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. It begins with an overview of essential foundations, including probabilistic models, variational inference, and other core concepts. The paper then delves into recent developments in generative adversarial networks, autoencoders, and related models, before discussing additional models topologically influenced models, normalizing flows, and non-factorized generative models. The paper also covers semi-supervised learning methods normalizing flows and non-factorized models. Finally, the paper concludes with a summary of performance comparison studies and future research directions in deep learning-based generative models.

This research introduces a data compression method rooted in a novel application of the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), tailored for 2-D image data. The approach merges data compression with error correction, yielding a system capable of recovering images after extreme distortion. Our results demonstrate that the BCAC approach outperforms state-of-the-art data compression methods in terms of visual recovery after compression, excels over alternative autoEncoders in terms of recovery quality, surpasses the need for a decoder, and surpasses the rate-distortion benchmark set by traditional compression methods.

We examine the thermodynamic properties of an Abelian gauge theory, specifically the SU(2) Yang-Mills theory, using lattice simulations in a wide range of temperatures. Our focus is on the critical point of the first-order phase transition and how it influences the power law behavior of the universal quantities. This study spans from a three-dimensional base to a nearly ten-dimensional system, allowing us to investigate the impact of the end point on the freeze-out, which occurs at a larger distance. The results are compared to non-Abelian gauge theories to explore how the two theories similarity varies over different scale sizes.

To comprehend the concept of saturation numbers, one must first understand saturation numbers of convex geometric hypergraphs.  Research concerning saturation in graphs and hypergraphs has been ongoing for nearly two decades and has been an area of active study for the last five years specifically within the context of convex geometric hypergraphs.  Previous research has demonstrated that certain classes of convex geometric hypergraphs exhibit non-trivial saturation numbers.  This dissertation aims to further explore the concept of convex geometric hypergraphs through the introduction of novel results, such as the presentation of upper and lower bounds for the saturation numbers of various classes of convex geometric hypergraphs, including those spanned by general geometric hypergraphs and trees, and the establishment of a lower bound for the saturation numbers of complete bipartite graphs.

This study involves analyzing the production cross-sections of $\alpha$ particles,
deuterons, and tritons at an intermediate energy of 127 MeV through a reaction with
a light target, specifically deuterium. The cross-sections are measured in the
range of forward angles. Notably, the cross-sections exhibit energy-dependent
variations, with the cross-sections in the angle range of 5.5-27.5 degrees showing
a significant rise with decreasing angle. The measured cross-sections for $\alpha$
particles are found to be an order of magnitude higher than those for deuterons.
The measurement process is validated by comparing the cross-sections with a Monte
Carlo simulation, and the findings are further supported by available literature
data. The study also presents the $A(E)$ curves for the angular distribution of the
generated cross-sections, with the findings showing a distinct production hierarchy
of $\alpha$ particles, deuterons, and tritons.

This study examines Trident, a 7cm climbing fish developed at Stanford University, 
alongside its natural counterparts: the Pacific Lamprey and Australian Garfish. 
Building upon previous research, Trident combines artificial muscles with active 
control to mimic the undulating motion used by fish for climbing. Observations 
show that Trident successfully navigates its leading edge into grooves, unlike the 
Pacific Garfish. Furthermore, video analysis reveals that Trident's climbing 
speed surpasses that of the Pacific Lamprey, despite the latter's extensive 
climbing experience. By studying both biological and artificial climbing fish, 
key principles for efficient progression have been identified, leading to the 
development of a new generation of robotic systems.

This study develops a computational model to simulate the combined effects of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy on colon cancer growth and immune response. The continuous tumor model is paired with a discrete stochastic model to follow individual cells and their responses to Doxorubicin. The IL-2 therapy is modeled separately, which helps to determine the most effective dosing schedule. By comparing both therapies individually and in combination, the researchers found that simultaneous administration is optimal. Doxorubicin and IL-2 together can significantly stimulate the immune system to fight cancer, even when doses smaller than those required for maximal tumor response are used.
